rows.defect: The dorsal sail is a grey dome floating above the back: at 3x its bottom edge is a hard, almost perfectly straight horizontal line that overhangs the spine, and the sail's grey is a completely different material from the mottled white body — nothing transitions. Its ribs are dead-straight 1px white lines. The two ears are perfect dark-grey circles, geometric primitives, giving the animal a Mickey Mouse head. The neck is the same constant-width lozenge with its rounded end visible over the shoulder. The legs are flat grey rectangles in a colour that belongs to no other part of the animal, with a visible offset kink at the knee and hard edges at both the belly and the hoof. The tail is the same detached bristle-brush as s16 and s18. The brown blotches are airbrushed clouds. This is the same rig as fauna-h2-s18 in this batch, only recoloured.
rows.fix: Fair the sail base into the dorsal ridge with a curved seam that dips below the back outline, carry the body's mottled skin into the lower third of the sail, and taper/clip the ribs to the membrane. Replace the circular ears with an asymmetric leaf shape rooted inside the skull silhouette. Recolour the legs to the body albedo and taper them (thigh 2x the cannon), filleting the top into the chest and haunch. Union the neck into the torso. Rebuild the tail as a tapering tuft grown from the rump. Differentiate the proportions from s18 so the two do not read as the same model.

rows.readsAs: a dragon-blood / banyan tree
rows.defect: This is not a fungus at all — it is a flat-topped canopy TREE. About twelve slender pale-green trunks fan outward from a narrow base and split into fine dichotomous twigs that fill a dome of foliage mass, with an elliptical cast shadow beneath. There is no stipe, no cap, no gills/pores/teeth, nothing fungal anywhere in the silhouette. The twig mass is drawn as leafless branch-fractal (a Dracaena/banyan crown), and it is byte-for-byte the same construction as s10 and s13 in this same batch.
rows.fix: Fix the router first: the fungi h2 height-class is dispatching into the tree/canopy branch renderer. Send fungi heights to a fungal builder (stipe + cap, or bracket shelf, or coral/clavarioid). If a giant 'hyphal thicket' macro-fungus IS the intent, the canopy must stop being foliage: thicken the branches monotonically toward a shared basal plate, remove the dichotomous twig-fractal, and terminate every tip in a fruiting body (cap, club or ostiole) instead of a leaf mass. Also make the seed pick a FORM CLASS, not just trunk count — s0/s10/s13 differ only in canopy width.

rows.readsAs: a morel or shaggy inkcap — the organism reads correctly, the surface does not
rows.defect: The bullet-shaped teal cap is covered edge-to-edge in a perfectly regular repeating diamond/chevron lattice at constant cell size and constant orientation. It does not compress or foreshorten as it approaches the silhouette edge and it does not wrap the dome, so it reads as a wallpaper texture sprayed over a flat shape rather than the fungus's own reticulate skin. The cap terminates in a dead-straight horizontal bottom edge, and the cream stem — a straight-sided tapered trapezoid with machined edges, no basal flare, no volva, no annulus — butts into it with a hard seam and zero transition. Two primitives stacked.
rows.fix: Drive the reticulation in cap-surface UV so the cells foreshorten and shrink toward the margin, and jitter cell size/rotation per-ridge so it stops reading as a tiled pattern. Break the flat cap margin: give it a slight downward-curling scalloped edge with per-sample noise. Grow the stem out of the cap — carry a few ridge lines down onto the upper stipe, add a basal bulb/mycelial fuzz at the ground contact, and add gentle width noise so the stem is not a clean trapezoid.

rows.readsAs: the same dragon-blood tree as s0, slightly bleached
rows.defect: Same tree as s0 — a whitish flat-topped crown on ~12 fanning trunks with fine dichotomous twigging, plus a few faint sparkle dots floating under the canopy. Nothing fungal is present: no stipe, cap, hymenium or substrate. Visually a near-duplicate of s0 and s13; the only deltas are a brighter foliage value and a marginally wider crown, so three of eight slots in this batch show the same organism.
rows.fix: Same router fix as s0 (fungi h2 must not reach the tree-canopy renderer). Separately, kill the free-floating sparkle dots under the canopy — they sit off-body in empty space with no emitter and read as engine debris. Then force seed divergence at the form-class level so consecutive fungi seeds cannot all resolve to one silhouette.

rows.readsAs: a nebula patch or a lump of blue-grey rock — not a living thing
rows.defect: An amorphous blue lump with a soft airbrushed fill, a lumpy freehand outline, and scattered pale dots — some inside the mass, many MORE outside it, forming a halo of loose specks in empty background around the whole blob. There is no anatomy of any kind: no cap, stipe, margin, gills, pores, hyphae, substrate contact or ground shadow. It has no top or bottom, no orientation, and no indication of scale. Unlabelled, no viewer would call this an organism.
rows.fix: Clip every speckle to the body mask — the off-body dot halo is a straight artifact and must be culled at the silhouette. Then give the form actual fungal anatomy: this looks intended as a resupinate crust/slime mold, so it needs a substrate to sit on (bark, log or rock), a raised gelatinous crown with a specular top light, a wet dripping lower margin, and internal plasmodial veining that follows the mass's flow direction instead of uniform random dots. Add a contact shadow so it stops floating.

rows.readsAs: two jellyfish perched on a branch
rows.defect: Two teal domes that are near-perfect geometric hemispheres, each with a hard dark crescent stroke running along the upper-left rim — that is an outline, not a form shadow, and it sits on top of the surface as a machined line. From each dome's underside hangs a curtain of straight teeth of near-identical width and round ends, all falling perfectly vertical and parallel, starting abruptly at a hard seam along the cap edge with no hymenial transition. They sit on a brown log that is a plain capsule: two straight parallel sides and two rounded caps, with a couple of straight scratch lines for bark.
rows.fix: Replace the hemisphere primitives with an irregular hydnoid cushion — asymmetric, lobed, with a slumping downhill side — and delete the rim outline stroke, replacing it with a soft terminator. Vary tooth length, thickness, and hang angle with the local surface normal so the teeth splay outward at the margin and shorten toward the centre, and blend their roots into the cap flesh so there is no cut line. Rebuild the log with a non-parallel tapering profile, a broken end, and bark texture that wraps its cylinder.

rows.readsAs: the same dragon-blood tree again
rows.defect: The third copy of the s0/s10 tree in this batch — pale flat-topped crown, ~12 splayed trunks, fine dichotomous twig-fractal, elliptical ground shadow, and a scatter of small dots floating in the gap between the trunks with nothing emitting them. Again zero fungal anatomy. Placed next to s0 and s10 a viewer would call all three the same species.
rows.fix: Same router fix as s0. Additionally remove the free-floating dots between the trunks (off-body artifact) and, once fungi are routed correctly, verify the batch by silhouette-diffing consecutive seeds — three identical crowns out of eight means the seed is only perturbing parameters inside one template instead of selecting between templates.

rows.readsAs: a clump of orange grass, or a stylised flame
rows.defect: A tuft of about eleven upright orange blades, each a smooth lens shape narrowing to a knife-sharp point, shaded with a clean vector gradient and no surface texture at all. Every blade is unbranched and every base is severed at one dead-flat horizontal line where the dark ellipse begins — they are cut off at the ground rather than emerging from it, so nothing is actually attached to anything. The whole cluster reads as blades of grass or a flame, not as flesh.
rows.fix: If this is a clavarioid/coral fungus, the clubs must branch and fuse near the base and end in blunt, rounded, slightly swollen tips — not knife points. Merge the bases into a shared fleshy foot with mycelial threads spreading into the substrate so the flat cut line disappears, splay the clubs in depth rather than all in one plane, and add a waxy subsurface gradient plus fine longitudinal wrinkling so the surface reads as fungal flesh instead of a flat gradient.

rows.readsAs: a purple bruise or a mineral stain — no organism is legible
rows.defect: The purple recolour of s11 — the same amorphous airbrushed lump, the same lumpy outline, the same dot field with a significant number of specks scattered OUTSIDE the body in the surrounding darkness. No cap, no stalk, no margin, no gills, no hyphae, no substrate, no cast shadow, no orientation. Two of the eight slots in this batch are this same featureless blob with the hue changed.
rows.fix: Cull all speckles to the body mask, then build actual anatomy as in s11 (substrate contact, raised gelatinous crown with specular highlight, dripping lower margin, flow-aligned plasmodial veins, contact shadow). Separately, s11 and s15 must not resolve to one shape with a hue swap — the seed needs to drive lobe count, spread direction and crown height, not just palette.

rows.readsAs: a river pebble or an unpeeled potato with glitter on it
rows.defect: There is no fungus in the picture. It is a single flat brown lump — a lopsided pebble outline with a soft airbrush gradient and a scatter of orange dots floating both on it and off it in the surrounding blackness. No cap, no stipe, no gills, no pores, no substrate contact, no depth: the form has one lighting pass and reads as a cutout. The dots are clearly sprayed on top of the shape rather than being pigment in a skin — dozens of them sit outside the silhouette entirely, drifting in empty background, which is the off-body-artifact failure. The outline itself is a low-poly polygon with several visibly straight chords (upper right and lower left edges are dead straight line segments meeting at hard corners).
rows.fix: This heightmap-2 'crust/slime' branch needs an actual fruiting structure, not a filled blob. Clip the speckle emitter strictly to the body path (no spawns outside the silhouette) and convert it from uniform dots to size-and-value-varied surface pigment that follows the form's shading. Break the polygon outline with per-vertex noise so no chord is straight, then add the thing that makes it a fungus: a lobed, guttating crust with a rolled margin and a differentiated underside, or a cushion with visible pore texture, plus a mycelial fringe where it meets its substrate.

rows.readsAs: a bunch of grapes, or soap bubbles stuck under a stick
rows.defect: A tapered brown bar crosses the upper third of the frame and a cluster of six pale-green balls hangs beneath it. The balls are perfect circles with a hard rim and a single glossy white ellipse highlight each — obvious geometric primitives, and the overlap lines between them are drawn as visible dark arcs, so it reads as stacked transparent spheres rather than one fused fungal body. The cluster does not grow out of the branch: the topmost sphere merely overlaps the bar's lower edge, with no attachment point, no basal fusion, no mycelium. The branch itself is a smooth machine-drawn lozenge with perfectly regular taper, no bark, no bud scars, and it terminates in mid-air on both sides with rounded end caps.
rows.fix: Replace the circle-stamping with a metaball/union pass so the caps fuse into a single continuous outline with only soft internal creases, and drop the per-sphere specular ellipse for a broad wet sheen that crosses several caps at once. Give each cap a slight asymmetry and a downward-tilted margin instead of a radius. Grow the cluster from the branch: a shared basal knot that swells out of the bark, bark texture and a wound/scar at the attachment, and let the branch exit the frame instead of ending in a rounded cap.

rows.readsAs: a bare winter shrub or a purple wire sculpture; plausibly coral fungus, but tree first
rows.defect: This one is close to reading correctly as a coral/antler fungus, and the dichotomous branching with fine terminal forks is genuinely good. What breaks it: the three stipes are perfectly straight machined cylinders of constant width with hard parallel edges and a dark outline down each side, and each one ends at the bottom in a flat cut-off — the stems stop dead rather than entering the ground, and the ground itself is a single flat black ellipse under them. Where each cylindrical stem meets its branching crown there is a visible seam: the cylinder shading (flat left-dark, right-light banding) stops abruptly and the branch strokes begin, so the crown looks socketed onto a post. Every branch is the same uniform stroke width with no thickening toward the trunk, giving a wireframe/armature look, and there are hard right-angle-ish elbows at several forks.
rows.fix: Taper and gently bow the stipes, thicken them toward the base, and swell them continuously into the first fork so there is no cross-section change at the junction — the crown must be the same tube widening, not a separate object. Scale branch thickness by depth (thick at the base fork, hair-fine at the tips) and round every fork into a Y-shaped crotch with fillet rather than a corner. Replace the flat black ellipse with the stems disappearing into duff/mycelial felt at their bases.

rows.readsAs: a clump of soap bubbles or jelly beads stuck to a twig — the same organism as fungi-h2-s17
rows.defect: Same construction as s17 and near-indistinguishable from it — a tapered brown bar with a ball cluster under it, recoloured teal. The five caps are perfect spheres with hard rims, and the overlap seams between them are drawn as strong dark arcs, so the mass reads as separate stacked balls. Worse than s17: the highlights are a row of five identical white ellipses marching diagonally across the top-left of the cluster like a decal, plus more scattered on the lower lobe — they ignore the individual spheres' curvature entirely and are the clearest 'sprayed on top' failure in the batch. Again there is zero attachment: the cluster floats beneath the branch, overlapping it, with no basal fusion and no bark wound. The branch is the identical smooth lozenge with rounded end caps hanging in mid-air.
rows.fix: Fuse the caps with a union/metaball silhouette and delete the internal arc seams. Derive highlights per-cap from that cap's own normal instead of stamping a shared ellipse row, and vary their size and opacity. Differentiate this seed from s17 — different cap count, tier layout, margin shape — because the two currently render as the same organism twice. Attach it: a swollen shared base emerging from bark, bark texture on the branch, branch running off-frame.

rows.readsAs: a bundle of matchsticks or cotton swabs planted in a chocolate coin
rows.defect: Seven perfectly straight, constant-width yellow lines fan up from a flat brown ellipse, each capped with a white ellipse that is stuck on the tip with a hard boundary — the stalk colour and the head colour meet at an abrupt line with no transition. The stalks are literal drawn line segments: no bend, no taper, no thickening at the base, and they pass straight THROUGH the substrate ellipse, with visible line stubs drawn on top of the brown ellipse's surface rather than emerging from it. The substrate is a perfect mathematical ellipse with a hard rim and a flat fill. Two of the heads sit at the picture edge in isolation with nothing behind them. Nothing about the surface says fungal tissue.
rows.fix: If the intent is a Marasmius/Mycena-type slender-stemmed group, the stalks must curve, taper (thicker at the base, thinner under the head), and vary in thickness between individuals. Swell each stalk into its head continuously — a cap has to flare out of the stem with a margin and an underside, not sit on it as a bead. Kill the perfect ellipse substrate: replace with an irregular noise-edged mound the stems root into (occlude the stem bases, do not overdraw them). Add gill or ridge structure under at least the nearer caps so the heads read as fruit bodies.

rows.readsAs: a cartoon sun, or a virus particle from a stock illustration — not a living fungus
rows.defect: A single geometrically perfect circle filled with a radial airbrush gradient, with six or seven flat isoceles triangles poking out of it at even angles, and one small dark grey dot dead centre. It is a primitive-and-decoration render: perfect circle body, machined straight-edged triangular spines with no taper curve, no thickness, no shading of their own, and each spine simply overlaps the circle's edge with a hard seam — none of them grows out of the surface. The centre dot reads as a pupil, giving the thing a face. Beneath it sits another perfect flat black ellipse for a shadow, which the body does not touch. There is no surface texture whatsoever.
rows.fix: Break the circle: puffballs and spiny earthballs are lumpy, flattened at the top, and pinched into a rooted base. Grow the spines out of the skin — each spine should share the body's surface shading, emerge from a swollen conical pad, curve, and vary in length and angle rather than radiating evenly. Add many more, smaller spines/warts across the whole surface rather than a handful of large ones on the perimeter silhouette. Remove the centred dot or convert it to a proper apical ostiole with a torn, raised, darker rim. Replace the ellipse shadow with contact shading where the base meets the ground.

rows.readsAs: cyan leaves or fish fillets pinned to a wooden plank — a decorative graphic, not an organism
rows.defect: The single worst piece in the batch. The 'trunk' is a literal dark rectangle — four dead-straight edges, perfect right-angle corners, running off the top and bottom of the frame with a flat two-tone fill and no bark, no curvature, no rounding. Attached to its right edge are five bracket shelves, but they are pointed almond/leaf shapes, all the same shape and same cyan gradient, stacked at nearly even vertical spacing like a repeated stamp. Each one abuts the rectangle's straight edge with a hard vertical cut — the seam is unmistakable, the shelves are pasted onto the plank, not erupting from it. Each shelf also carries a thin dark hairline stroke floating above it that reads as a stray drawn line rather than a shadow or an edge. The whole composition is flat, front-lit, and fills the frame edge to edge with no negative space.
rows.fix: The substrate must be a tree, not a box: irregular silhouette, bark ridges, curvature, and a diameter that varies. Shelf fungi must swell OUT of the bark — model each bracket with a thick swollen root of tissue that fans into the trunk (occluding the bark, casting a wedge of contact shadow), a rounded outer margin (not a leaf point), a visible pore-bearing underside, concentric growth zones across the top, and randomized size/tilt/spacing so no two are the same stamp. Vary the palette across the shelves and delete the floating hairline strokes.

rows.readsAs: a moss-covered rock or a lump of green clay — the same organism as fungi-h2-s16
rows.defect: A recolour of s16 with the identical failure. A single amorphous green polygon lump, soft airbrush gradient, no cap, no stipe, no gills, no pores, no attachment to anything. Bright green dots are scattered over it AND well outside its silhouette into the black background — several are 60-80px clear of the body, floating in space, which is the off-body-artifact defect again. Multiple outline segments are perfectly straight polygon chords with hard corners, especially along the top-right and bottom-left. The dots are all the same size and full-brightness regardless of where they fall on the form, so they sit visibly on top of the shading instead of being lit by it.
rows.fix: Same as s16, plus differentiation: this seed and s16 currently render as one organism in two colours. Clip the speckle emitter to the body path, size- and value-modulate the specks by the local shading, and noise the outline so there are no straight chords. Then give it real fungal morphology — a lobed crust or cushion with a rolled margin, a differentiated underside, guttation droplets that read as wet volumes rather than flat dots, and a mycelial fringe anchoring it to a substrate.

rows.readsAs: a cartoon tortoise icon / a toy car with a dome shell
rows.defect: The two legs are free-floating rounded-rectangle blobs sitting BELOW the shell with a clear black gap between them and the body — nothing connects them to the animal; they read as two wheels under a car. The plastron is a flat slab with a dead-straight machined horizontal edge running the full width. The carapace pattern is a wireframe of perfect concentric arcs plus radial spokes drawn ON TOP of the dome (a drafting diagram, not scutes — real scutes are polygonal plates with relief and a raised ridge between them). Head is a plain ellipse with a hard-edged short cylinder overlapping it as a neck; the seam where that cylinder meets the shell rim is a visible straight cut. Eye is a perfect circle with a perfect white annulus. No feet, no toes, no tail.
rows.fix: Attach the limbs: extend each leg mass up INTO the plastron so the outlines merge, and give it a foot with 3 blunt toes at ground level. Replace the concentric-arc grid with 5-6 irregular polygonal scute plates (vertebral row + costals), each shaded individually with a slight bevel so the pattern is relief, not line-art. Break the plastron's straight bottom edge into a shallow scalloped curve. Blend the neck by drawing it as a tapering mass that starts inside the shell opening rather than an ellipse butted against the rim.

rows.readsAs: the same tortoise as s0, painted silver — a chrome turtle ornament
rows.defect: Identical geometry to fauna-h0-s0 with a blue-grey palette swap — same half-dome, same concentric-arc wireframe, same flat plastron slab, same two detached blob legs floating below with a visible gap. It is not a distinct organism, it is a recolour. On top of that the near-monochrome silver-on-navy value range makes the shell wireframe the only readable feature; the body reads as a glass paperweight. Head ellipse + cylinder-neck seam is again a hard straight cut at the shell rim.
rows.fix: Same structural fixes as s0 (weld limbs to the body, real scute plates, scalloped plastron, blended neck), PLUS force divergence from s0: this variant needs a different shell profile (flatter/keeled), different limb count or limb form, and a value range that separates the shell from the background — currently the silver dome sits at nearly the same luminance as its own highlight.

rows.readsAs: a cartoon dachshund crossed with a jackrabbit — clearly a friendly dog-thing, not an alien
rows.defect: A quadruped rig with only TWO legs drawn — one front stub and one rear stub, both on the same side; the far pair is entirely absent, so the animal has nothing holding up its other flank. Both legs are comically short stubs (roughly 1/6 of body depth) under a very long capsule barrel whose dorsal line is a straight ruler edge from shoulder to rump. There is a visible pale arc seam where the neck mass overlaps the barrel at the shoulder. The tail is a bristle fan clearly glued to the rear cap — the brush strokes start at a hard boundary rather than emerging from tapering flesh. The nose is a perfect black circle.
rows.fix: Draw the far limb pair at reduced value/saturation for depth. Lengthen the legs to at least 1/3 body depth or, if a dachshund proportion is intended, add carpal/tarsal joints so they read as deliberately short rather than truncated. Kill the shoulder arc by drawing neck and barrel as one continuous outline. Taper the tail base into the rump over ~20px so the bristles grow out of a fleshy root. Make the nose an asymmetric wedge with a nostril slit instead of a circle.

rows.readsAs: a jellyfish, or at second glance a mushroom cap on many stems
rows.defect: There is a stray four-sided PARALLELOGRAM outlined in thin dark line on the upper-left of the bell — a leftover stroked path with four dead-straight edges and sharp corners sitting on the creature's skin. It is unmistakably a rendering artifact, not anatomy. Beyond that: the bell's bottom is a dead-straight horizontal rim across its whole width, and every tentacle butts against that flat line rather than emerging from bell tissue. The three pink markings are flat, perfectly circular, uniformly filled discs of different sizes that read as stickers applied on top, with no shading following the dome's curvature.
rows.fix: Find and remove the stray quad stroke (looks like an un-cleared path from a panel/facet pass). Replace the straight bell rim with a gently scalloped margin and let the tentacle roots swell into the bell (a small triangular fillet at each junction). Reproject the pink spots as ellipses foreshortened by the dome normal, with soft edges and a subsurface glow, so they sit IN the bell rather than on it.

rows.readsAs: a cartoon red cow or spotted deer with glow-in-the-dark stickers
rows.defect: Bioluminescent glow blobs sit OFF the body: a large soft white haze floats in empty background above and left of the withers, well outside the silhouette, with two of the perfect-circle light points inside it hanging in mid-air. Only two legs are drawn for a quadruped. Both legs are hard-edged angular sticks whose upper segment is a darker rectangle with a straight vertical edge butted under the belly — a visible seam at the shoulder and hip, and the elbow is a sharp polygonal kink rather than a joint. The barrel's dorsal line is a straight ruler edge. The dark spots are uniform scattered ellipses that ignore the body's form and read as sprayed on. The two horns are straight white cones stuck flat onto the cheek, and the two 'ears' are two perfect dark circles overlapping the skull outline.
rows.fix: Clip the glow haze to the body silhouette (mask the bloom pass by the creature alpha) and place every light point on a surface. Add the far limb pair. Rebuild legs as continuous tapering masses that widen into the shoulder/haunch mass so there is no seam, with a rounded stifle instead of a corner. Warp the spot field along the body's UV so spots compress toward the flank edges. Grow the horns from a fleshy boss on the frontal bone and curve them; replace the circle-ears with tapered pinnae attached along a line, not a point.

rows.readsAs: a salmon-coloured camel-stegosaurus toy; near-identical rig to fauna-h0-s14
rows.defect: The eye is broken — instead of an eye there is a small cluster of black flecks/scribble on the side of the head, no pupil, no iris, no lid. The neck is a separate straight-sided cylinder laid over the shoulder: you can trace its full outline crossing the chest, a hard overlap seam where it meets the body. The dorsal spine plates are separate rounded ellipses sitting behind a hard outlined arc on the back, each with its own boundary — they read as balloons parked on the spine, not as bony processes growing from it. The glow bloom again spills outside the silhouette (a haze under the belly floating over background). The head is a shapeless lump with two perfect dark circles for ears and a cone snout.
rows.fix: Fix the eye primitive (it is degenerating to a scatter of dots) — one sclera, one iris, one specular. Merge neck into thorax: one continuous outline, no cylinder edge crossing the chest. Rebuild dorsal plates as triangular processes rising OUT of the back contour (the back line should deform up into each plate), not ellipses behind a line. Mask the bloom to body alpha. Give the skull a defined cranium/muzzle break instead of a lump.

rows.readsAs: an almost-invisible grey camel with balloons on its back; a desaturated clone of s13
rows.defect: The five dorsal plates float DETACHED above the back — each is a rounded capsule separated from the body by a visible pale line running the length of the spine, with background-dark gaps between them; nothing grows out of the animal. The whole render is critically under-lit: charcoal grey on navy, the body is barely separable from the background and the four legs disappear into black at the ground. The legs are plain capsules butted under a straight belly line with a value break at each junction (visible seams at all four shoulders/hips). The tail is a bristle brush terminating in a bare perfect white circle — a naked primitive with no shading. The eye is a perfect circle, the ears are two perfect dark circles, and this is the same quadruped rig as s13 with a grey palette.
rows.fix: Weld the plates: raise the dorsal contour itself into each plate so the back line and the plate share one silhouette, and remove the pale separating stroke. Lift the whole value range at least 25-30% — the darkest fauna still needs a rim light to clear the navy background. Blend leg roots into the torso mass. Remove or reshade the white circle at the tail tip (it should be a tuft, not a ball). Differentiate the rig from s13 (plate count, neck length, body depth) so the two are not palette twins.

rows.readsAs: a dart or a paper arrow — at best a headless dead fish; a stranger would not name an organism
rows.defect: This does not read as an animal at all. There is no head and no eye — the right end simply terminates in two thin rods with rounded club tips sticking out into space. The tail is two flat triangular BLADES with perfectly straight machined edges and sharp points, like fletching on a dart. The body is a lumpy grey-green tube with a hard cream outline stroke along the top. Composition is broken: the subject sits in the lower-right, roughly the bottom third of the frame, leaving about 60% of the 440x440 canvas empty, and it is very low contrast against the dark ground. Worst of all there are THREE small vertical tick marks floating in empty background at the far left, well away from the creature — stray off-body artifacts with nothing to attach to.
rows.fix: Remove the three floating tick marks (orphaned stroke pass). Add a head: a distinct cranial mass with at least one eye at the anterior end, and resolve the two club-tipped rods into either antennae rooted in that head or a proper limb pair. Replace the straight-edged triangular blades with a curved, membranous caudal fin whose rays fan from a fleshy peduncle. Re-centre and re-scale the subject to fill the frame like the rest of the batch. Raise the value contrast — the body currently sits only a few steps above background.

rows.readsAs: a clump of teal ornamental grass or a small agave / aloe rosette
rows.defect: Nothing fungal is present. Seven teal blades, each a perfectly symmetric pointed-lens shape with a smooth left-to-right gradient, rise from a flat dark ellipse. No cap, no stipe, no gill, no spore surface. Every blade is the same shape at four scales and two rotations, and each one is cut off by a dead-straight horizontal line at the base where it meets the ground ellipse — a hard seam, not a growth junction. The blades are flat: the only shading is a linear gradient running across the width, so they read as cut paper, not as flesh.
rows.fix: Give the fungal archetype an actual cap/stipe: swell the top third into an asymmetric cap with a rolled or ragged margin and a darker underside, and taper the stipe toward the base with a small basal flare. Kill the straight bottom cut — flare the last ~20px of each stalk outward into the substrate with a mycelial fan so the silhouette never crosses a horizontal line. Break the blade template: vary the curvature, tip bluntness and edge noise per instance instead of scaling one path.

rows.readsAs: four pink surfboards or magnolia petals glued to a wooden plank
rows.defect: The substrate is a literal rectangle — two dead-straight vertical edges, dead-straight top and bottom, uniform width, with a lighter rectangular stripe inset that is also perfectly straight. It is a geometric primitive, not a trunk. The four brackets are the same symmetric pointed-ellipse path repeated at four scales; each one meets the rectangle in a hard vertical seam (the shelf's left edge is a straight cut flush with the rectangle's right edge — no fusion, no swelling, no shadow of attachment). The pale curved hairlines on each shelf sit on top of the pink gradient like a decal rather than following the form, and the thin dark hairs along each shelf's upper edge float free of the surface.
rows.fix: Replace the rectangle with a painted trunk: irregular bark silhouette with bowed edges, vertical fissure noise, no straight lines. At each bracket, widen the shelf base into a wedge that flares INTO the trunk over ~15-25px and paint a contact shadow plus a slight bulge of bark around it so the join is a fusion. Make the shelves asymmetric half-fans (wider outboard, kidney-shaped margin) rather than mirrored lenses, and drive the concentric zone rings as displaced copies of the shelf's own outline so they curve with the form.

rows.readsAs: a bare winter shrub or a stand of dead saplings in orange
rows.defect: Reads as dead vegetation rather than fungus. Four separate stems stand as near-parallel uniform-width tubes with rounded pill ends and a visible horizontal join where each tube meets the branching mass above it — a stuck-on seam. The tubes have no taper at all from base to fork, and the twigs above are all the same hairline thickness regardless of branch order, so a terminal twig is as thick as the limb carrying it. The whole crown is a flat tangle of straight line segments with no thickness hierarchy and no volume, sitting on a flat dark ellipse shadow.
rows.fix: Taper radius along every branch (child radius ~0.7x parent) so twigs thin toward the tips, and remove the flat cap on the stems by continuing the same tapered stroke through the fork rather than butting a tube against the crown. Curve the stems — no two should be parallel — and vary their base separation and lean. If this is meant to be coral fungus, thicken and fleshy-ify the branches with blunt antler tips and a shared fused base instead of four discrete twiggy trunks.

rows.readsAs: the same picture as fungi-h2-s7 recoloured — four orange planks/petals on a wooden post
rows.defect: Morphologically identical to fungi-h2-s7 in the same batch — same rectangle trunk with the same inset stripe, same four mirrored pointed-lens shelves at the same four positions and scales, same decal hairlines. Only the hue differs (orange instead of pink). All of s7's construction faults are present: machined rectangle, hard vertical seam where each shelf abuts the trunk, symmetric lens shelves, and free-floating dark hairs above each shelf edge.
rows.fix: Same trunk and attachment fixes as s7, plus decorrelate the two species: drive shelf count, vertical spacing, tilt, outline asymmetry and trunk lean from the species seed so two fungi in the same family do not share a traced silhouette. Hue must not be the only per-species variable.

rows.readsAs: a fluorescence-microscopy field of a bacterial smear, not a single organism
rows.defect: The cell body is a polygon: the faint dark silhouette running across the frame has visibly straight facet edges and hard corners (clearest along the top-left and lower-right), which no cell has. The blue glow is a set of soft round blobs painted independently of that outline, so the luminous mass and the body edge disagree — the glow spills well outside the silhouette on the left. The pale rod marks are scattered uniformly at random with identical length and random rotation, which reads as spray, not as internal structure. On the right edge two thin blue flagella-like curves start OUTSIDE the body with a visible gap and connect to nothing.
rows.fix: Replace the faceted hull with a closed spline (subdivide and jitter the vertices, no segment longer than a few px) so no straight edge survives, and clip the glow to that hull with a soft inner falloff. Root the two right-side flagella at a point on the membrane and thicken them at the base so they emerge from it. Give the rods a purpose — align them along a flow field or cluster them around the granules — instead of uniform random scatter.

rows.readsAs: nothing identifiable — a barely-visible grey smudge; on close inspection a flat amoeba pictogram
rows.defect: Essentially invisible. The body is a dark grey blob only a few values above the near-black background; at normal viewing you see almost nothing. Inside it are four flat, perfectly circular discs of slightly lighter grey at three sizes — plain geometric primitives with no shading, no membrane, no nucleolus. The silhouette is outlined by a uniform 1px hairline stroke that reads as vector linework, and it has one hard pointed corner on the right where the outline kinks. There is no cilia, no flagellum, no cytoplasmic texture — just a grey teardrop with dots.
rows.fix: Raise the body value and saturation hard — this archetype needs a real fill (a translucent cytoplasm with a rim-lit membrane) so it separates from the dark card. Drop the uniform hairline outline in favour of a soft thickness-varying membrane with a brighter rim on the light side. Replace the flat circles with shaded organelles (gradient, offset highlight, irregular vacuole outlines) and add internal cytoplasmic granulation plus surface locomotion structures so it reads as alive.

rows.readsAs: nothing identifiable — the same barely-visible grey smudge as microbe-h0-s1
rows.defect: Same failure as microbe-h0-s1 and near-indistinguishable from it: a nearly black-on-black grey blob with a 1px hairline outline and four flat perfect-circle discs inside, only the blob outline and the dot positions differ slightly. No contrast against the card, no membrane rendering, no internal texture, no cilia or pseudopod detail. Two of the circles overlap into a figure-eight that reads as a Venn diagram rather than as organelles.
rows.fix: Same as s1 — lift value/saturation so the cell is actually visible, paint a real membrane with rim light instead of a stroke, shade the organelles. Additionally, decorrelate s1 and s10: change blob elongation, organelle count and arrangement, and locomotion structures per seed, because right now the two are the same drawing with the outline nudged.

rows.readsAs: a string of dough balls or a bunch of grapes in front of a sunburst graphic
rows.defect: The cilia are a starburst decoration, not anatomy: roughly a hundred dead-straight lines of varying length all radiate from one point BEHIND the cell chain, so they pass through and past the body irrespective of where the membrane is, and several rays on the left originate in empty space with no body to attach to. They are pure straight segments with no curve, taper or flick, which reads as a sunburst clipart layer. The body is four perfect circles with identical airbrush spherical shading, decreasing in size along an arc; the overlaps are hard circle-on-circle intersections with no fusion at the joins. The dark lens on the largest sphere reads as a mouth or blowhole.
rows.fix: Root each cilium on the membrane itself — sample points around the outline of the fused body, emit from the normal, and give each a slight taper and a curved (sine-phased) shaft so they beat rather than radiate. Never draw one behind the body from a shared centre. Fuse the spheres with a metaball / union so the joins swell instead of intersecting, deform each cell off-round, and remove or re-purpose the dark lens so it does not read as a mouth.

rows.readsAs: A glass marble or a green pea. Nobody would say 'microbe'.
rows.defect: A mathematically perfect circle, olive-khaki, with a thin uniform grey ring outline and — the worst part — a DEAD-STRAIGHT horizontal chord at about 60% height, below which the fill jumps to a flat saturated green. That straight line cutting the body in two is a machined edge, not biology; it reads as the waterline in a snow globe or the paint line on a marble. Two hard white specular dots (one large perfect circle top-left, one tiny) sit on top of the surface as stickers rather than as light on a wet membrane. No cytoplasmic structure, no membrane thickness variation, no flagellum, no polarity — nothing that says 'alive'.
rows.fix: Kill the chord: replace the straight-line fill split with an irregular internal organelle mass (a lobed, off-centre blob with feathered edges), or if it must read as a fluid level, warp the boundary with 3-4 octaves of noise and give it a meniscus. Break the circle: perturb the outline radius with low-frequency noise (±6-9%) so the silhouette is an ovoid, not a compass circle. Vary the outline stroke width around the perimeter and let it fade where the light hits. Replace the hard specular dots with a soft elongated highlight following the curvature. Add at least one asymmetric feature (a flagellum growing out of the wall with a thickened base, a contractile vacuole) to establish that this is an organism and not a bead.

rows.readsAs: A dandelion clock, or a string of pearls sitting on a sunburst logo.
rows.defect: The body — a chain of four cream spheres decreasing in size, coccus-chain style — is actually the best-formed silhouette in the batch, but it is buried under a starburst of roughly 120 perfectly straight black rays radiating from a single centre point out to a uniform radius. They are drawn BEHIND the body and do not touch it: they emanate from a point in space, not from the cell wall, so the cilia look like a background sunburst graphic the sphere-chain was pasted onto. They are also all the same length and dead straight, which no cilium is. Separately, a hard-edged dark grey ellipse sits on the front sphere like a punched hole (a mouth?), with no lip, rim, or shading transition — a decal. The four spheres also meet at hard tangent creases with no fused membrane between them.
rows.fix: Re-root the cilia: emit each one from a point ON the outer contour of the sphere chain, with a thickened base that shares the body's cream colour and tapers to a dark tip, and give each a slight sinusoidal curve with randomised length (±40%) and phase so the field reads as beating, not as a compass rose. Cull the ones currently drawn over empty space away from the body. Replace the punched dark ellipse with a soft-shouldered depression (inner shadow + faint rim highlight) or delete it. Fuse the spheres with a metaball/blend so the junctions get a fillet instead of a tangent crease.

rows.readsAs: A badminton racket, or a charcoal grill grate seen from above. Not any living thing.
rows.defect: This is not a drawing of an organism, it is a wireframe diagram. A geometrically perfect ellipse outline (thin, uniform-width grey stroke) contains: one dead-straight horizontal axis line spanning the full width, three identical small white dots on that axis (left end, centre, right end), and roughly 30 perfectly vertical, evenly spaced, equal-thickness straight tick marks hanging off it. Every element is a primitive: perfect ellipse, straight lines, uniform spacing, perfect circles. There is no fill, no volume, no shading, no interior, no light source. Nothing grows out of anything — the ticks are struck through the ellipse and stop at nothing.
rows.fix: Start over from mass, not from line art. Give the cell an actual filled, shaded body with a noise-perturbed ovoid contour. If the ticks are meant to be cilia, root them on the membrane, curve them, vary length and spacing, and taper them; do not run them as chords through the interior. If the horizontal line and three dots are a spine/nuclei, they need to be internal structures rendered with depth (soft-edged nuclear blobs seen through translucent cytoplasm), not a schematic axis with endpoint markers. At minimum: no perfect ellipse, no straight lines, non-uniform stroke.

rows.readsAs: A golf ball, or a ball of Cheerios glued together.
rows.defect: A pale blue-white sphere plastered with ~40 identical stamped decals: each is a flat perfect ellipse containing two perfect concentric rings. They are sprayed ON the surface rather than being the creature's own skin — the ones near the rim stick out past the silhouette as flat coins seen edge-on, which betrays that they are billboarded sprites, not surface features. They do not shrink or foreshorten correctly toward the limb of the sphere, they are all the same size and same orientation-agnostic ellipse, and none of them deform to the curvature. The underlying body is a perfect circle with almost no terminator shading, so the whole thing reads flat despite the sphere intent.
rows.fix: Make the pattern belong to the skin: project the discs onto the sphere so they foreshorten and compress into thin lenses at the rim, and clip them at the silhouette rather than letting them protrude. Randomise their diameter (±35%), ring count and ring eccentricity so they stop reading as one stamp repeated. Add real spherical shading — a terminator, ambient occlusion where discs overlap, subsurface glow — so the volume is carried by light, not by the pattern. Perturb the outer contour off perfect-circle. Consider making the protruding rim discs into actual 3D bosses/pores with their own cast shadows if they are meant to be surface organelles.

rows.readsAs: Three hot dogs, or three earthworms with a bead threaded on each.
rows.defect: Three near-identical orange-red rods lie in horizontal stripes across the frame, and all three are CLIPPED by the canvas edges — the top one runs off the right edge, the bottom two run off both left and right, so the organism has no complete silhouette. Each rod is a capsule: uniform diameter, perfectly rounded caps, an airbrushed cylinder gradient with a specular strip along the top, i.e. exactly the capsule primitive that should never appear. Stuck at the midpoint of each rod is a sphere bead of a different, brighter colour with a hard circular boundary — a ball glued onto a sausage, with no fillet, no shared shading, no continuity of the surface pattern across the join. The faint ladder of parallel cross-hatch ticks only appears on the left half of each rod and stops abruptly at the bead, another hard seam. Repeating the same body three times as parallel stripes reads as a wallpaper tile, not as a colony.
rows.fix: Pull the whole composition inside the frame with margin — nothing should touch the canvas edge. Break the capsule: taper the rod ends asymmetrically (one blunt, one drawn out), vary the diameter along the length, and bend the centreline with noise instead of a single smooth arc. Dissolve the bead join with a metaball blend so the swelling grows out of the rod and shares its gradient and its segmentation ticks continuously across the junction. Carry the cross-hatch segmentation the full length of the body and wrap it around the curvature instead of stopping at the bead. If a colony of three is intended, vary their length, thickness, angle and colour and let them overlap in depth rather than stacking as parallel horizontal bands.

rows.readsAs: An amoeba, or a spilled drop of gravy. The organism reads correctly — the craft does not.
rows.defect: The strongest read in the batch — a soft rust-brown amoeboid blob with an irregular, non-circular contour and a dark nucleus, which genuinely suggests a cell. But: the value is so close to the near-black background that the lower-left third of the body dissolves entirely and the form is barely legible; the whole silhouette is traced with a thin, perfectly uniform-width orange rim stroke that reads as a vector outline laid over the paint rather than as rim light (it does not vary or drop away on the shadow side); and the interior 'vacuoles' are three overlapping mathematically perfect circles of flat semi-transparent grey with hard edges, sprayed on top of the cytoplasm with no refraction, no shading and no relationship to the body's own light. There is also an unexplained small notch/nick on the right contour that looks like a rendering artifact rather than a pseudopod. The shape is symmetrical and static — no pseudopod extension, no direction of travel.
rows.fix: Raise the body value 25-35% against the background so the full silhouette is legible, and add a cool bounce or ambient term on the shadow side. Make the rim light directional: strong on the lit upper-left, fading to nothing on the lower-right, with varying thickness — or drop the uniform stroke entirely and let the value edge do the work. Rebuild the vacuoles as soft-edged, slightly ovoid inclusions with an inner shadow and a small specular kick so they sit INSIDE the cytoplasm; jitter their radii and stop them being concentric-perfect circles. Extend one or two pseudopods with thickened bases so the cell has a direction and reads as motile. Resolve or remove the notch on the right edge.

rows.readsAs: A nebula, a Bunsen flame, or a smoke-brush Photoshop texture. Not an organism at all.
rows.defect: There is no organism here, only a field. A purple fog fills nearly the whole 440px canvas and its boundary is a RECTANGLE — you can see straight, axis-aligned top, bottom and left edges to the haze where the noise field was clipped to its bounding box, which is a hard machined edge and instantly reads as a texture swatch. Scattered inside are ~200 tiny purple dashes (all the same length and thickness, random rotation) and ~15 flat grey circles, none of which are contained by any membrane or connected to anything — they are confetti over a gradient. On the right edge, three or four thin curved purple lines hang in the void OUTSIDE the fog mass with nothing to attach to: off-body artifacts with a visible gap between them and the form. There is no silhouette, no body, no scale cue, no light.
rows.fix: Give it a body first: define an enclosing membrane contour (irregular, noise-perturbed, well inside the frame with margin) and clip the fog, the dashes and the granules to it so they read as contents of a cell rather than as a background. Never clip a noise field to its rectangular bounding box — always mask it with the organism's own alpha. Re-attach the loose curved lines to the membrane with thickened, shaded bases, or delete them. Vary the dash length, width and value so the granulation reads as organelles at different depths, and add depth cueing (blur/desaturate the far ones). Add a light direction so the mass has a lit side and a shadow side.

rows.readsAs: A handful of white pills or Tic Tacs spilled on a table.
rows.defect: Twelve literal capsules — the exact rounded-rectangle/pill primitive the brief forbids — scattered at random angles on empty black. Every one has the same uniform width, the same perfectly hemispherical caps, and the same generic top-left airbrush gradient regardless of its rotation, so the lighting contradicts itself across the group. They are entirely disconnected: no membrane, no colony matrix, no substrate, nothing holding the picture together, so it reads as spilled objects rather than as one creature. Several simply cross each other in X shapes with hard overlaps and no interaction, contact shadow or squash. A few carry a single thin straight dividing line (a septum?) that is drawn as a flat 1px stroke across the pill, another machined edge. Two at the bottom-left overlap almost exactly, which reads as an accidental duplicate rather than a dividing cell.
rows.fix: Break the capsule: give each bacillus a slightly bowed centreline, unequal end caps (one rounded, one squarer), a subtle waist or bulge along the length, and per-instance length/width variation of ±40%. Light them from a single shared direction so the gradient rotates with the body. Bind the field together — a faint translucent slime matrix or biofilm halo enclosing the group, plus soft contact shadows where they overlap and slight deformation at contact points. Replace the flat septum line with a pinched constriction in the silhouette itself (an actual waist in the outline plus an inner shadow) so division is read from the form. Vary hue/value slightly per cell so they read as individuals at different depths, and separate the coincident pair at bottom-left.

rows.readsAs: a blackberry, or a ball glued over with translucent poker chips
rows.defect: The silhouette is a mathematically perfect circle, and the 'cells' covering it are ~40 identical perfect ellipses each stamped with 2-3 concentric rings. They read as decals laid on a ball, not as cells bulging out of a shared envelope — every disc has the same tilt-family, the same ring count, and a hard outline that does not deform where discs overlap. The discs on the rim (left edge ~x=135, bottom ~y=300) are drawn as complete free-floating ellipses that break the sphere outline with hard edges rather than being cross-sections of cells at the horizon. There is no interior depth: the cyan highlight in the middle sits under the discs like a lamp rather than being membrane sheen.
rows.fix: Break the outer circle — jitter each rim cell's contribution to the silhouette so the outline is lumpy (morula/blackberry), not a circle with bumps. Kill the concentric rings entirely; replace with one soft off-axis specular highlight per cell plus a faint nucleus blob whose offset varies per cell. Vary cell diameter 0.6x-1.4x and let overlapping cells flatten each other at contact (draw contact as a shared crease, not two stacked outlines).

rows.readsAs: sparks blowing off a campfire, or a smeared gram stain — not one organism
rows.defect: There is no organism here. The subject is a soft amber cloud with no silhouette that runs off the left and right frame edges (clipped at x=0 and x=440) — it is a background, not a body. Scattered inside are ~150 tiny hard-edged rod dashes and about eight flat grey discs, all sitting on top of the blur with no relationship to it. Worst: the long curved filaments on the right (from roughly x=300 out to x=440, y=120-300) emanate from empty dark space — they are attached to nothing, the classic off-body artifact. Nothing in the frame is a creature you could point at.
rows.fix: Give it one body. Collapse the cloud into a bounded mat/colony blob with a defined, irregular margin that fits inside the frame with a 40px gutter. Root every filament in that margin — trace each one from a visible basal cell on the outline, tapering from ~4px at the base to a hair at the tip, and delete any strand whose origin is not inside the body mask. The rods should be embedded (drawn under a translucent envelope layer, sharing its light) rather than blitted on top.

rows.readsAs: a fat orange hamster, or a plastic tardigrade toy
rows.defect: The head is a separate circle pasted onto the right end of the body: a hard, unbroken pale outline runs right through the overlap (around x=270, y=180-235), so you can see the full circle behind the body edge. That is a seam, not a neck. The body itself is a plain egg with the segmentation drawn as five straight vertical scratch lines that ignore the body's curvature and stop dead before the outline — sprayed on. All four legs are identical stubby trapezoids butted against the underside with flat tops; none of them grow out of the body wall. The drop shadow is a flat blurred ellipse that floats detached to the right of the rear foot.
rows.fix: Boolean-union the head into the body and re-stroke a single outline around the combined mask, then indicate the neck with a shading crease only. Redraw the segment lines as curved bands that follow the dorsal arc, wrap over the silhouette edge, and are rendered as a light/dark shading pair (raised segment) rather than a single dark stroke. Taper each leg from a wide base that continues the body contour, vary the four leg lengths/angles, and re-seat the shadow directly under the foot contact points.

rows.readsAs: the same animal as s4 in a different colour — a mint hamster
rows.defect: This is microbe-h0-s4 with the hue rotated from orange to mint — identical outline, identical head-circle position, identical five scratch lines, identical four leg stubs, identical shadow. Two entries in one batch that differ only in fill colour is a distinctness failure on its own. It also carries every s4 defect: the head disc's full circular outline is visible crossing the body at ~x=272, and the vertical segment lines are straight strokes that die before reaching the silhouette.
rows.fix: Beyond the s4 fixes (union the head, curve and wrap the segment bands, taper the legs into the body), drive real shape variance off the species seed — body aspect ratio, dorsal hump position, head size relative to body, leg count/spread, cuticle texture — so two microbes on the same archetype never share a silhouette. Colour must not be the only seeded axis.

rows.readsAs: a glass marble, or a bubble half-filled with pea soup
rows.defect: A perfect geometric circle with a crisp 2px ring stroke, filled olive-tan on top and dark green on the bottom, split by a dead-straight horizontal chord at y=245. It reads as a container with liquid settled in it, not as living tissue. The three white dots and one larger white blob are perfect circles floating at random with no shading relationship to the sphere. The subject occupies only ~28% of the frame width and is otherwise empty — there is no morphology at all: no membrane irregularity, no organelles, no motility structures, nothing.
rows.fix: Delete the straight chord — if this is meant to be a cytoplasm/vacuole boundary, make it a curved meniscus that bulges with the membrane and feathers at the edges. Replace the perfect circle with a seeded irregular closed spline (5-8% radius wobble) and drop the uniform ring stroke for a rim-light that varies in weight with the light direction. Add actual content: a nucleus with a visible envelope, granular cytoplasm noise, and at least one motility feature (flagellum or cilia band) rooted in the membrane. Scale the body up to ~65% of frame.

rows.readsAs: a string of blue beads, or a molecular model render
rows.defect: Three chains of flawless, identically-sized spheres, each with the same specular dot in the same relative position — it is a ball-and-stick render, not a cell chain. The spheres merely overlap; there is no shared cell wall, no flattening at the contact points, no septum where daughter cells divide. The composition is three disconnected fragments floating with a large empty right-bottom quadrant and the upper-left chain running out of frame at the left edge (x=30). The Y-junction at the left is two chains crossing rather than a real branch.
rows.fix: Flatten each cell against its neighbours so contacts become straight septa and the chain gets a continuous outer wall (draw the chain as one union mask, then shade individual cells inside it). Vary cell diameter along the chain and randomise the highlight direction per cell instead of copying it. Recompose to one dominant chain filling ~70% of the frame with fragments as supporting detail, and pull the left chain fully inside the frame.

rows.readsAs: a lens flare or pin-cushion starburst with some ping-pong balls in the middle
rows.defect: The cilia are a starburst of ~70 dead-straight dark lines radiating from a single point, and they are not attached to the animal. The rays converge on a centre near (238,215) but the body cluster sits offset from it, so on the lower-left the rays clearly begin in empty background well away from any cell, and on the right they pass straight over the large sphere and continue out the other side. They are also DARKER than the background near the hub, so they read as scratches on the lens, not as hairs. The body is four perfect spheres of decreasing size overlapped with hard visible arcs where each meets the next — pure stacked primitives, no shared membrane. The large dark ellipse on the front sphere is a flat hole with no rim or depth.
rows.fix: Root every cilium on the body outline: sample points along the union silhouette, emit each hair from its own point along the local surface normal, and clip anything that starts off-body. Give them curvature (slight sine bow, tip taper) and a metachronal phase offset so they are not a radial fan. Make them lighter than the background, not darker. Union the four spheres into one mask, shade lobes with soft creases instead of hard arcs, and give the pore a raised lip plus interior shadow.

rows.readsAs: three glowing zip ties, or measuring tapes laid out on a bench
rows.defect: Three capsule silhouettes — long tubes with perfectly hemispherical end caps — which is exactly the banned rounded-capsule shape. The segmentation is a ladder of straight, evenly-spaced, identical-thickness cross rungs running the full length like a zipper or a bandsaw blade; the rungs do not curve with the tube or vary in spacing. Each tube has a sphere pasted on it (top one at x=245, middle at x=135) whose full circular outline is visible sitting proud of the tube — a hard seam, and it serves no readable anatomical purpose. The bottom tube has a duplicate darker rod overlapping its right end (x=305-415) that reads as a render ghost, and its cap ends mid-air over the lighter body. All three are near-parallel arcs of the same length and colour.
rows.fix: Break the capsule: taper the anterior and posterior to different profiles (blunt head, pointed tail) and let the body diameter swell and pinch along its length. Replace the ladder rungs with annuli that curve around the tube's cross-section, vary in spacing (tighter near the ends), and are shaded as raised rings (light edge + shadow edge) rather than single strokes. Either union the mid-body sphere into the tube as a real swelling (clitellum-style, blended shading, no outline) or delete it. Remove the ghost rod on the bottom specimen. Vary the three specimens' length, curvature and thickness, and overlap/foreshorten them so it is a group, not three parallel copies.

rows.readsAs: a grove of dragon's-blood trees, or a head of broccoli
rows.defect: Best picture in the batch, but it is not a fungus — the "cap" is fine dichotomous TWIG branching (a canopy of thousands of hairline forks), so there is no pileus surface, no rolled margin, no gills/pores/veil anywhere. The seven stems are constant-width round-cap strokes with zero taper from base to fork, and every base ends in a blunt flat stub that stops ~4px ABOVE the ground shadow ellipse — nothing touches the substrate. Scattered pale dots float in the black negative space between the stems (visible around x=200-330, y=250-290) with no emitter; they read as dust on the lens, not spores.
rows.fix: Taper the stems (w = w0*(1-t)^0.7) and flare each base into a 3-5 finger mycelial foot that overlaps the shadow ellipse. Swap the twig-canopy generator for a fungal cap: one solid pileus path with a downturned margin and radial lamellae visible under the rim, keeping the branch structure only as internal veining. Either delete the free-floating specks or anchor them to a spore-fall emitter under the cap rim so they trail downward.

rows.readsAs: a bundle of orange pipe cleaners, or a wireframe coral model
rows.defect: Parts are stuck on, not grown out. At 3x the four trunks are perfectly parallel-sided capsules of literally constant width with rounded end caps and no taper, each with a hard dark outline down one side — extruded plastic tubing. Every fork is a separate stroke laid OVER the trunk: at each Y-junction you can see the darker branch stroke crossing the lighter trunk as an overlap seam instead of emerging from it. Twigs terminate in blunt round caps in mid-air. No cap, no gills, no fungal tissue of any kind; the stem bases float clear of the shadow.
rows.fix: Stop stroking with lineWidth. Emit a tapered polygon per segment (child width = 0.62 x parent) and draw trunk-through-child as ONE continuous path so no stroke ever overlaps another; add a swelling collar of ~1.3x parent width at each junction. Replace round end caps with pointed tapers. Sink the bases into a basal pad. Then add actual fungal anatomy — this generator is producing a shrub.

rows.readsAs: a marble, a small moon, or a ping-pong ball
rows.defect: A geometric primitive: one mathematically perfect circle (~65px radius) filled with an airbrush radial gradient. No stem, no cap, no substrate — the sphere floats above a detached soft ellipse shadow with a clear gap. The grey speckles are flat uniform-opacity dots sprayed on top; they are the same size and same spacing at the limb of the sphere as at the centre, so they sit on the picture plane rather than on a curved surface.
rows.fix: Replace the arc() with a closed lumpy path: 10-14 radial control points jittered +/-12% with a low-frequency noise term, and squash the vertical axis to ~0.85 so it is not a ball. Give it a stipe or a basal mycelial attachment that overlaps the shadow. Turn the speckles into warts with their own lit/shadow side, and scale each dot's radius and spacing by the cosine of the surface normal so they crowd and flatten toward the limb.

rows.readsAs: a naval contact mine, or a virus icon from a stock illustration
rows.defect: Perfect circle + straight-edged isoceles triangles drawn BEHIND it. At 3x each of the eight spines meets the body at a hard circular boundary with no basal swelling and no fusion — they are stuck on, and the spine edges are dead-straight machined lines with flat uniform fill. A perfect flat circle is punched into the centre as an "eye", which pushes it further from fungus and toward a creature/icon. The body does not touch its own shadow ellipse.
rows.fix: Build ONE silhouette path: widen each spine base to ~30% of its length and blend it into the body with a quadratic curve rather than an abutting straight edge, then union body+spines before filling. Vary length, angle and curvature per spine off the seed instead of an even radial fan. Remove the centre dot or make it a genuine pore/ostiole with depth. Deform the body off-circle and give it a substrate contact.

rows.readsAs: the same naval mine as s5, repainted bone-white
rows.defect: Identical to fungi-h1-s5 with the palette swapped from teal to cream — same perfect circle, same eight flat triangular spines at the same angles, same punched centre dot, same floating body over a detached shadow. Every s5 defect is present, plus the batch now shows two species that are the same picture in different paint. It is also the third sphere in eight (s4, s5, s6, s9).
rows.fix: Same structural fix as s5 (union the spines into the body path, curved swelling bases, deform the circle). Additionally, drive spine COUNT, length ratio, curvature and body eccentricity from the species seed, not just hue — right now the seed only reaches the colour ramp. And add a non-sphere branch to the fungi router so four of eight variants are not balls.

rows.readsAs: a handful of buttered popcorn under a floating chocolate bar
rows.defect: Off-body artifact. A dark brown horizontal bar (the branch/log) floats across the upper third with a wide band of pure black between its underside and the top of the fungus — roughly 30px of nothing. The fruiting body is a cluster of smooth overlapping ellipse lobes with plastic airbrush highlights, and thin dark vector arcs are drawn over the top that cross straight through lobe boundaries and, at the lower right, spill OUTSIDE the silhouette edge into the background. Sprayed-on decoration with no clipping.
rows.fix: Attach it or delete it: the branch should pass behind the upper lobes with the lobes' contour deforming and swelling around the contact, plus a shared occlusion shadow. If the branch cannot be attached, remove it from the composition entirely. Clip all surface detail to the body path, and make the arc strokes lobe-local (one arc set per lobe, terminating at that lobe's edge) rather than one arc field over the whole cluster. Break up the two hard specular ovals.

rows.readsAs: a clump of purple grass, or a cluster of amethyst crystal shards
rows.defect: At 3x every one of the nine blades is cut off by a razor-straight HORIZONTAL line at the base, all at very nearly the same y — a machined guillotine cut. The blades are separate detached slivers with black gaps between them and a black gap below them before the shadow ellipse starts; there is no shared base, no mycelial mat, nothing they grow out of. Each blade is a flat facet with straight parallel-ish sides and a single hard white specular streak, which reads as injection-moulded plastic. No cap, no gills, no fungal structure.
rows.fix: Give them a common origin: a lumpy basal mass or mycelial pad that all blades emerge from, its lower contour sunk into the shadow ellipse, with each blade's base widening into that mass over its lowest 20%. Curve the blade spines (currently near-straight) and vary width per blade. Replace the single specular streak with broken, surface-following highlight so the facet stops reading as plastic.

rows.readsAs: two grey river stones, or a pair of bowling balls
rows.defect: Two mathematically perfect circles overlapping. The right circle's edge cuts a hard crescent seam across the left circle's body — they overlap rather than merge, so it reads as two objects, not one organism. Each carries a hairline bright rim-light stroke along its upper-left that just STOPS mid-arc with a blunt square end, a stroke artifact sitting on top of the form. Speckles are flat dots at constant size and density right up to the limb, so they sit on the picture plane. No stem, no cap, no gills; the bodies float above a detached ellipse shadow.
rows.fix: Replace both arc() calls with jittered irregular blob paths and union them with a metaball/smooth-min so the two lobes share ONE silhouette with a fillet in the crotch instead of one circle occluding another. Delete the abrupt hairline rim stroke — do rim light as a clipped gradient along the body path so it fades out. Foreshorten the speckles toward the limb. Anchor the lower contour into the shadow. Add at least one fungal read: a pore surface, a basal stipe, or a split veil.

rows.readsAs: A handful of dried spaghetti or paper drinking straws with pearls glued on — an inanimate bundle, not an organism
rows.defect: Five long tan/orange rods lie almost parallel across the full 440px width, crossing each other. Each rod is a perfectly uniform-width capsule with hemispherical rounded caps and no taper from base to tip, and each is covered in evenly-spaced perpendicular tick marks that sit on the surface like printed ruler graduations rather than reading as cell walls or septa. A small glossy sphere is stuck onto each rod partway along its length with a hard circular seam — the bead does not swell out of the filament, it overlaps it like a pasted marble. Nothing here is a body: there is no cell, no membrane, no centre, just five detached sticks and five detached beads. Two of the rods (upper-left dark brown, mid-left dark brown) are also nearly the same shape as the bright ones, so the whole picture reads as repeated stamps of one primitive.
rows.fix: Kill the constant-width capsule: drive rod radius from a per-filament profile that swells at the bead and tapers to a fine point at both ends so the bead IS the filament's own bulge, not an overlaid sphere. Replace the regular perpendicular ticks with irregular, curvature-following segment boundaries drawn as shading breaks (darker crease + lighter ridge) rather than hairlines. Reduce to 2-3 filaments and curve them independently so they no longer read as a parallel bundle.

rows.readsAs: A bunch of grapes or a clutch of eggs sitting in front of a spray of pine needles
rows.defect: The body is a clump of six or seven identical smooth spheres of two sizes piled together — the joins are pure overlap with visible crescent shadows, so it reads as separate balls in a heap rather than one organism. Behind it is a corona of perfectly straight dark hairlines radiating from a single point roughly at the clump's centre; they are machined straight rays, all the same length, and because they originate at one interior point they pass behind and through the sphere cluster instead of emerging from the membrane. They are also nearly the same value as the background, so the cilia halo half-disappears. Two flat dark ovals sit on the two largest spheres as sprayed-on spots with no rim or depth.
rows.fix: Emit cilia from sampled points ON the outer silhouette with an outward normal, each with slight curvature, varying length and a taper from a thicker root to a fine tip; lift their value above the background so they register. Fuse the sphere cluster into one continuous membrane (union the blobs and re-shade the merged silhouette so there is a single specular family) instead of stacking independently lit spheres. Give the dark ovals a lip/shadow so they read as pores or vacuoles rather than paint.

rows.readsAs: Sperm cells / flagellate protozoa — correct, but reads as clip-art rather than painted
rows.defect: Best-reading image in the batch — four teardrop flagellates on a diagonal, and the overall gesture is convincingly alive. But the flagella are uniform hairline strokes that begin abruptly at the body outline: there is no basal thickening and no taper into the cell, so each tail reads as a wire touching the body rather than growing out of it. The nucleus in each cell is a flat, perfectly circular red dot with no shading, no membrane and no interaction with the body gradient — it looks stamped on. The bodies themselves are perfectly smooth two-stop gradients with zero surface incident, and all four are the same teardrop with only scale changed, so they read as four copies of one stamp.
rows.fix: Taper the flagellum: 3-4px at the root fading to sub-pixel at the tip, and start it inside the body silhouette so the join is hidden under the body shading. Give the nucleus/eyespot a soft edge, an off-centre highlight and a faint darker halo so it sits inside the cytoplasm. Add per-instance variation to the body outline (slight asymmetry, a kink, differing tail-neck length) and some low-amplitude cytoplasmic mottling.

rows.readsAs: A badminton racquet, or a technical schematic of a comb jelly — a diagram, not a creature
rows.defect: This is a wireframe diagram, not a painted organism. A geometrically perfect orange ellipse outline sits on the dark field with a dead-straight horizontal axis line through it, terminated by a small dot at each end and one at the centre, and filled with a regular picket fence of straight vertical hatch lines of graded height. There is no volume, no shading, no interior, no lighting — the shape is entirely line art and you can see the background through it. Every element is a geometric primitive: perfect ellipse, perfect line, evenly spaced parallel strokes.
rows.fix: Give the cell an actual painted body: filled translucent cytoplasm with a rim-lit membrane, an irregular (not analytic) ellipse outline, and interior organelles with depth. If the vertical strokes are meant to be comb rows or cilia, curve them, vary their spacing and length, root them on the membrane and shade them; delete the straight axis line and the three endpoint dots entirely, which read as CAD construction geometry.

rows.readsAs: A green glass marble or a snooker ball
rows.defect: A single perfect circle, filled with a green sphere gradient, ringed by a thin uniform grey stroke, with one round specular highlight top-left. A dead-straight horizontal chord slices across the lower third, below which the green is a flat darker block — a hard machined edge with no relation to the sphere's curvature. Three tiny white dots float in the middle with no depth. The result is a billiard ball / bubble, and it is also very small in a 440px frame, occupying maybe a quarter of the width with a large empty margin.
rows.fix: Break the perfect circle — perturb the silhouette with low-frequency noise so the membrane is organic. Delete the straight chord (or replace it with a curved, soft-edged internal boundary that follows the sphere, e.g. a settled vacuole with a meniscus that bows). Turn the white dots into shaded inclusions/granules. Enlarge to fill the frame like the other members of the batch.

rows.readsAs: A wireframe ellipse / drawing-compass diagram — the same object as s11 in a different colour
rows.defect: Pixel-for-pixel the same construction as s11 with the colour swapped from orange to white/grey: perfect ellipse outline, dead-straight horizontal axis line with a dot at each end and one at centre, regular picket fence of straight vertical hatch strokes, no fill, no shading, no volume. Two organisms in one batch that differ only in hue is a variation failure on top of the diagram problem — and in white it reads even more like an engineering drawing.
rows.fix: Same as s11 (paint a filled, rim-lit body; curve and root the strokes; remove the axis line and endpoint dots), plus give this seed a genuinely different morphology from s11 — change the aspect ratio, the row count, the row orientation, add asymmetry — so the two are not recognisably the same stamp.

rows.readsAs: A string of pearls or a twisted balloon-animal — approximately streptococcus, but reads as beads rather than tissue
rows.defect: A branching Y-shaped chain of blue-violet balls. The chain gesture is good and the branch point is a believable idea, but every element is a perfect circle with an identical shading ramp and highlight, and where two touch there is a hard crescent shadow — so the chain reads as separate marbles laid in a line, not as one filament of joined cells. There is no shared membrane, no flattening at the contact points (real coccal chains squash where they touch), and no continuity of the light across the chain. The junction where the three arms meet is a pile of overlapping balls rather than a structural fork.
rows.fix: Union the cells into a single metaball silhouette so adjacent cells flatten against one another and share one continuous rim light; keep only a soft crease at each septum instead of a hard crescent. Vary cell diameter and roundness slightly along the chain. Resolve the branch point into one larger mother cell that the two arms visibly emerge from.

rows.readsAs: A green marble — indistinguishable in kind from s12
rows.defect: Again a single perfect circle with a sphere gradient, a thin uniform grey ring outline, one round top-left specular, three tiny flat white dots, and a straight horizontal chord across the lower third with flat darker green beneath it. It is the same construction as s12 with a slightly more saturated green and marginally different dot placement — two blockers in one batch that are the same object. Small in frame with a wide empty margin.
rows.fix: Same as s12 — perturb the silhouette off perfect-circle, remove or curve the straight chord, give the granules depth, fill the frame. Then differentiate this seed from s12 structurally (different granule count/arrangement, different internal boundary shape, different aspect), not just by hue.

rows.readsAs: Three model-aircraft propeller blades with a spinner hub, or bent hair-clips with a bead threaded on. Not obviously alive.
rows.defect: Three violet rods, each with a PERFECT CIRCLE bead sitting on it at mid-length. The bead is a separate, lighter-value sphere with its own independent specular highlight and a visible hard edge where it overlaps the rod — a textbook 'part stuck ON rather than growing OUT of the body' seam. The rod itself does not swell, pinch or deform to meet it; the outline of the circle is continuous straight through the join.
