On top of that the rods carry perfectly evenly-spaced ladder rungs (short transverse ticks at constant pitch, constant length, constant grey value) that run right up to the rod's edge and stop dead — that is a sprayed-on hatch pattern, not the creature's own segmentation, and the pitch does not compress toward the tapering ends the way real annuli would. Silhouette of each rod is a bent capsule with hemispherical caps. The middle and bottom rods also have a hard tonal break at the bead: bright lilac on one side, near-black plum on the other, with no gradient across the boundary, so each one reads as two different objects clipped together.
rows.fix: Delete the discrete bead primitive and instead drive the bead as a local radius bulge on the rod's own centreline spline (widen the width profile over ~15% of arc length with an eased in/out), so it is one continuous outline with no overlap edge. Kill the constant-pitch tick loop; replace with annuli whose spacing scales with local rod width (denser at the tapers), whose stroke alpha varies per-ring, and which curve to follow the rod's cross-section rather than being straight chords. Make the bright/dark halves one continuous lighting ramp along the rod instead of two flat fills meeting at the bead.

rows.readsAs: A glass marble, or a spirit-level bubble vial seen end-on. Nobody would say 'cell'.
rows.defect: This is a geometric primitive, not an organism: one mathematically perfect circle with a 1px uniform grey outline all the way round, a glassy radial gradient, and a single hard-edged elliptical specular dot at upper-left. Cutting across it at exactly the horizontal is a dead-STRAIGHT machined line separating an olive upper half from a darker green lower half — a fluid level, not biology. Two tiny white dots float near the highlight. There is no membrane irregularity, no cytoplasmic texture, no organelle, no flagellum, no pseudopod, nothing that varies around the perimeter. It also occupies only about a quarter of the 440px frame, floating small and centred with vast empty background.
rows.fix: Perturb the boundary — drive the outline from a noised radial function so no two radii match, and let the outline stroke vary in weight and drop out entirely in places. Replace the straight fill line with a curved, feathered internal boundary (a nucleus or vacuole with its own soft edge), or drop it. Add interior structure that belongs to the cell (granules, a nucleoid, ER-like striation) rather than a glass highlight, and kill or heavily soften the specular so it stops reading as polished glass. Scale the body up to fill ~65-75% of frame.

rows.readsAs: A green glass marble — the same marble as s7 and h2-s0.
rows.defect: Same defect set as microbe-h1-s7, and visually a near-DUPLICATE of it in the same batch — identical perfect circle, identical size and position, identical grey rim, identical upper-left specular blob, identical dead-straight horizontal fluid line, identical tiny white dots. The only differences are a slightly greener hue and one extra small dot. Two organisms in one batch that a viewer cannot tell apart is a generation failure, not a variant. Also the same tiny-in-frame problem (~25% of canvas).
rows.fix: As s7 (noised outline, curved internal boundary, real cytoplasmic content, kill the glass specular, scale up). Separately, the variation axis for this morph is clearly doing almost nothing — widen it so it also drives outline eccentricity, organelle count/placement, and overall silhouette, not just hue, otherwise sibling seeds will keep colliding.

rows.readsAs: Spirochete bacteria (Borrelia / Leptospira) — correct read, this one lands.
rows.defect: Genuinely the strongest image in the batch: four coral helices with fine tapering hair-thin ends that thin out organically and fade rather than stopping at a cap — no seam anywhere, and the terminal filaments clearly grow OUT of the coil. Real defects are compositional and rhythmic. (a) The helix pitch and amplitude are near-constant along every coil, so each one reads as a machined spring; real spirochetes vary wavelength along their length and between individuals. (b) The upper-left and centre individuals overlap and cross into a knot, so at a glance the picture reads as one tangled mass rather than four organisms. (c) All four have essentially the same coil count and the same tone, so they read as stamped copies of one asset rotated.
rows.fix: Modulate wavelength and amplitude along the arc (e.g. multiply the sine by a low-frequency noise envelope) and vary coil count and body thickness per individual. Add a depth/tone offset so the rearmost individual is dimmer, and re-lay the composition so the two upper individuals do not overlap.

rows.readsAs: A glass marble again. If you showed s7, s8 and s0 side by side people would call them the same object in three shades.
rows.defect: The third identical marble in one batch. Perfect circle, uniform grey rim, glass radial gradient, hard specular dot upper-left, four small white dots, and the same dead-STRAIGHT horizontal line splitting the disc into a lighter top and a flat darker-green bottom. Indistinguishable at a glance from microbe-h1-s7 and microbe-h1-s8. No membrane variation, no organelle, no appendage, no texture; the 'contents' are a flat fill with a ruler edge. Small in frame with a large empty border.
rows.fix: Same structural fix as s7/s8 — noised, variable-weight outline; curved feathered internal structure instead of a straight fill boundary; real interior granularity; remove the glass specular; enlarge to fill the frame. Then fix the generator: three seeds producing the same picture means the coccoid branch has essentially one output, so give it distinct sub-forms (diplo/tetrad/irregular, budding, capsule halo, differing organelle load).

rows.readsAs: A beaded plastic necklace bent into a triangle, or a 'play' arrow made of gumballs. Streptococcus is the intent but the corner kills it.
rows.defect: A chain of teal balls, but every ball is a PERFECT CIRCLE with the identical canned shading — same highlight position, same terminator, same rim — repeated ~18 times, so it reads as one sprite stamped along a path. Where they touch there is no fusion at all: each circle's outline is drawn complete and they simply overlap, giving hard crescent seams between beads instead of the pinched septa a dividing chain actually has. Worse, the path itself is angular — it runs down-left, hits a sharp near-90-degree corner at bottom-left, kicks back up-right, and throws a second straight spur off to the right, producing a triangular arrowhead. That is a machined polyline, not a filament with bending stiffness. Two beads at the top-left are doubled/overlapping in a way that looks like a rendering mistake rather than a bud.
rows.fix: Replace the stamped circle with a metaball / union fill so adjacent cells merge into a single outline with pinched waists at the joins, and vary each cell's radius and lighting slightly. Drive the chain along a smooth C2 curve with a minimum bend radius (no corner tighter than ~3 cell diameters) and drop the branching spur, or make it a proper Y-fork with a widened junction cell. Fix the doubled beads at the head of the chain.

rows.readsAs: A green nebula, or a smear of pond scum / mould on a slide. Nobody would name a single creature.
rows.defect: There is no organism here — it is a diffuse green fog occupying almost the whole 440px frame with no membrane, no silhouette and no coherent body. Inside the fog float roughly a hundred tiny green dashes at random angles plus about a dozen flat grey circles, all of which read as SPRAYED-ON confetti: the grey discs in particular have no shading relationship to the cloud, sit at uniform opacity, and look like dust on the lens. Thin pale filaments appear only along the right-hand edge and only there — they start abruptly out of empty haze with nothing to attach to, so they read as stuck-on whiskers on a cloud rather than flagella on a body. The blob's edge is a soft airbrush falloff that touches the canvas border on three sides, so the picture also has no framing.
rows.fix: Give it an actual body: a defined (irregular, noised) outer membrane the fog lives inside, with the glow as internal cytoplasm rather than the whole subject. Anchor the filaments to visible basal points on that membrane and distribute them around the perimeter, not only on the right. Reduce the dash count by ~70% and make them follow internal flow lines / vary in scale with depth instead of uniform random scatter, and either remove the flat grey discs or re-render them as shaded vacuoles that respond to the same light direction. Pull the whole thing in to ~75% of frame so it has a border.

rows.readsAs: Pharmaceutical capsules / white pill halves scattered on a table, or sticks of chalk. Reads as objects, not bacilli.
rows.defect: Nine identical white CAPSULE silhouettes — perfect stadium shapes with exactly hemispherical caps, constant width along the entire length, no taper, no bend, no surface incident — scattered at random rotations on black. This is the literal capsule-primitive failure. All nine share the same shading recipe (cool grey along the lower-left flank, white along the upper-right) and, apart from three that have a small straight hairline septum, the same length, so they read as one asset instanced nine times rather than nine individuals. Two of them intersect at a hard T-junction near the bottom-right with a visible overlap edge and no fusion. There are no flagella, no pili, no polar caps, no membrane texture, no colour variation — the surface is a plain vertical gradient with nothing organic on it.
rows.fix: Break the primitive: build each rod from a slightly curved spline with a width profile that is not constant (fatter mid-body, subtly asymmetric poles) and a boundary carrying low-amplitude noise so no two rods share an outline. Vary length by ±30% and give each its own light response and hue offset. Replace the straight septum with a pinched constriction that actually narrows the outline. Add at least one surface cue — polar granules, faint striation, or a few fine flagella growing out of the poles as tapering strands. Resolve the T-junction overlap into a proper crossing with depth (dim the rear rod).

rows.readsAs: A tardigrade (water bear) plush — or a grey-legged hippo
rows.defect: This is not a microbe, it is a pale blue-white tardigrade toy, and it is the same mesh as s5, s8 and s9 with only the hue swapped (4 of the 8 organisms in this batch are literally this same picture). Beyond the duplication: the head is a separate smaller oval pasted onto the right flank with a visible hard crescent seam where its outline crosses the body — the neck does not exist, the lobe just overlaps. The four legs are flat grey tapered triangles in a DIFFERENT colour from the body, butted against the underside with a hard straight edge and zero muscle mass or hip swell; they read as cardboard tabs glued on. The two eye/mouth spots are perfect dark circles. The body silhouette is a near-perfect ellipse and the segment 'folds' are hairline single-weight strokes laid on top of the gradient — they cast no shadow and do not deform the outline, so they are sprayed-on pinstripes rather than cuticle rings.
rows.fix: Fuse the head lobe into the body with a shared outline and a tapering neck mass so no crescent seam is visible; recolour legs to the body albedo with a darkening gradient at the join and add a hip/coxa bulge that pushes the body silhouette outward at each leg root; give the segment lines width variation plus a paired shadow so they read as folds, and notch the dorsal outline at each fold; deform the eye circles into asymmetric ocelli. Most importantly, drive the hue AND the topology from the species seed so s2/s5/s8/s9 are not the same model recoloured.

rows.readsAs: A bunch of grapes or a cluster of marbles with a spark/starburst effect behind it
rows.defect: A cluster of five perfect spheres with pure radial-gradient shading (they read as glass marbles or ball bearings, not cells), sitting in front of a starburst of ~90 dead-straight dark spines. The spines are the worst part: they radiate from a single geometric centre point, they are perfectly straight with no taper or curve, and most of them DO NOT TOUCH THE CELL at all — there is a wide empty gap between the inner ends of the spines and the sphere cluster on the left and lower-left, so the burst floats behind the body as an off-body graphic. They also render as near-black lines darker than the background vignette, which makes them look like a scratch/spark VFX layer rather than cilia or a pilus coat. The spheres themselves are joined by simple overlap, each with its own complete circular outline and its own highlight, so the colony is five separate balls, not one organism. One sphere carries a single dark oval 'mouth' blob that appears on no other sphere and has no lip or structure.
rows.fix: Anchor every spine to a point on the actual cell wall (root them per-sphere, normal to the local surface) and delete the shared centre-origin; taper each spine root-to-tip, add slight curvature and length jitter, and lighten them to a translucent mint so they read as cilia. Merge the spheres with a metaball/union pass so the colony has one continuous outline and the highlights read across the group instead of five independent specular dots. Break the perfect circularity with 3-6% radial noise. Remove the lone dark oval or give every cell a matching structure.

rows.readsAs: Flagellate protozoa or sperm cells under a microscope — correct family
rows.defect: The strongest render in the batch — five cream flagellated cells with red nuclei and long wavy flagella; it genuinely reads as a protozoan/flagellate field. Two real problems remain. (1) The small cell at upper-right has NO flagellum while all four of its siblings do, and one long wavy strand in the mid-left passes through open space without attaching to any body, so there is a spare detached tail floating in frame. (2) The five bodies are the identical symmetric teardrop primitive at five rotations/scales — same taper, same pointed tip, same centred highlight — which makes them read as stamped copies rather than a population. The red nuclei are perfect saturated circles that sit on top of the cream gradient with no surrounding cytoplasm darkening, so they look like dots painted on.
rows.fix: Give every cell exactly one rooted flagellum and clip any strand whose root is not on a body; vary the body outline per-cell (asymmetric bulge, one blunt-tipped, one bent) instead of rotating one primitive; soften the nucleus edge and add a faint halo/vacuole so it sits inside the cytoplasm.

rows.readsAs: A green tardigrade / water bear — indistinguishable from s9, s2 and s8
rows.defect: BYTE-IDENTICAL to microbe-h2-s9 (both md5 e2e0fefb4c5d1f3b482175a1c58ddc43) — the exact same PNG is shipped for two different species IDs, same mint-green tardigrade, same pose, same pixels. It is also the same mesh as s2 and s8 with a hue swap. All the s2 construction faults are present verbatim: the head is a smaller oval overlapped onto the right flank with a hard crescent seam and no neck; the four legs are flat tapered triangles butted onto the underside with a straight-edged join and no hip mass; two perfect dark circles serve as eye and mouth; the dorsal silhouette is a plain ellipse; the segment lines are hairline strokes painted over the gradient that neither shadow nor notch the outline. It is also not microbial — it reads as a small mammal-sized animal, and the soft cast shadow under it implies a lit floor, which fights the 'microbe' name.
rows.fix: First, make the seed actually vary the geometry so s5 and s9 cannot emit the same bytes — vary segment count, body aspect, leg count/length and head size, not just hue. Then fix the shared mesh: merge the head into the body outline with a tapered neck, root the legs in body-coloured hip swells that bulge the silhouette, give the folds width and shadow, and de-circularise the eyes.

rows.readsAs: A marble, a bubble, or a half-filled ball — nobody would say 'organism'
rows.defect: This is not an organism at all — it is a flat olive-green disc. Perfect circle, single thin light-grey ring outline of uniform weight, filled with a smooth linear gradient. Inside sits a darker green half-disc whose top edge is a razor-straight horizontal chord running the full width of the circle — a machined line, no cell has that. On top are one large perfect white circle and four tiny perfect white dots as 'vacuoles', all with hard edges and no refraction or depth. There is no cytoplasm texture, no membrane thickness variation, no organelle, no asymmetry anywhere. Occupies maybe 25% of the frame with nothing else to read.
rows.fix: Delete the straight chord — replace the settled-mass shape with a lobed, irregular vacuole cluster whose boundary follows a noise curve; break the outer circle with membrane undulation and vary the outline weight around the perimeter; give the vacuoles elliptical distortion, rim light and a soft inner shadow so they read as inclusions inside a volume; add granular cytoplasm texture and at least one distinguishing structure (nucleoid, pseudopod bulge, flagellum) so it is identifiable as a cell rather than a sphere.

rows.readsAs: Giardia or a pair of flagellate protozoa — right family, but the two cells read as overlapping stickers
rows.defect: Two golden teardrop cells with red nuclei and three long wavy flagella. The family reads correctly, but the two bodies are joined by plain overlap — the right cell's full outline crosses the left cell's face as an unbroken hard edge, so it looks like one sticker laid over another rather than two cells in contact or one dividing cell. Flagellum count does not match body count: the left cell carries two tails and the right one, with no visible basal body or root thickening at any of the three attachment points; each tail simply begins as a hairline at the body edge, tangent to it, which is the classic stuck-on join. Both bodies are the same perfectly symmetric leaf primitive, one just rotated. The metallic gold gradient with a bright centred specular makes the cells read as polished brass leaves rather than living cytoplasm, and the red nuclei are hard-edged perfect circles sitting on the surface.
rows.fix: Either merge the two bodies into one continuous outline (a dividing cell with a cleavage furrow) or separate them so no outline crosses another body; thicken each flagellum at its root and sink it into a small basal swelling on the cell wall; asymmetrise the two body outlines so they are not the same rotated leaf; desaturate the metallic specular toward a translucent cytoplasmic sheen and soften the nucleus edge.

rows.readsAs: A pink tardigrade / water bear toy — the same creature as s2, s5 and s9
rows.defect: Same tardigrade mesh as s2, s5 and s9, this time in hot pink — the fourth appearance of one model in an eight-organism batch. Identical construction faults are visible: the head is a smaller oval overlapped onto the right flank, its outline cutting a hard crescent seam across the body with no neck between them; the four legs are flat tapered triangles butted onto the belly line with a straight-edged join and no hip or shoulder mass, so they read as glued-on tabs; the eye and mouth are two perfect dark circles; the body is a clean ellipse; the segment lines are hairline strokes over the gradient that neither shadow nor notch the outline. The pink is a flat saturated hue with no subsurface variation, which makes the whole thing read as moulded plastic, and there is a cast floor shadow under a supposed microbe.
rows.fix: Vary the geometry per seed rather than the hue — different segment count, body aspect, leg length and head proportion — so this stops being s2 in a different colour. Then fix the shared mesh: fuse head into body with a tapered neck and single continuous outline, root the legs in body-coloured hip swells that bulge the silhouette, give the folds width plus a paired shadow and a matching notch in the dorsal outline, and break the eye circles into irregular ocelli. Add subsurface hue variation so the pink is not a flat plastic fill.

rows.readsAs: A green tardigrade / water bear — the exact same picture as s5
rows.defect: BYTE-IDENTICAL to microbe-h2-s5 (both md5 e2e0fefb4c5d1f3b482175a1c58ddc43) — literally the same file, same mint-green tardigrade, same pose, same pixels, shipped under a second species ID. Two species that render to the same bytes is an outright generator failure, not an art nitpick. It also shares the mesh with s2 and s8, so half this batch is one model. The mesh faults: the head is a smaller oval pasted onto the right flank with a visible hard crescent seam and no neck; the four legs are flat tapered triangles butted onto the underside with a straight-edged join and no hip mass; eye and mouth are perfect dark circles; the body is a plain ellipse; the segment lines are hairline strokes over the gradient with no shadow and no notch in the outline. Plus a cast ground shadow under something called a microbe.
rows.fix: Trace why the seed for s9 produces the same output as s5 — the seed is clearly not reaching the geometry parameters, only (at best) the palette. Make segment count, body aspect, leg count/length/splay, head size and fold spacing all seed-driven. Then repair the shared mesh: continuous head-into-body outline with a tapered neck, body-coloured legs rooted in silhouette-bulging hips, folds with width and shadow, irregular ocelli in place of circles.

rows.readsAs: A puff of cigarette smoke with white lint in it. Nobody would say 'living thing'.
rows.defect: There is no organism here — no membrane, no silhouette, no body. It is a field of ~15 overlapping soft grey gaussian blobs with hard-edged white dashes scattered across it like lint, plus exactly four thin whisker curves leaving the RIGHT edge only (two upper, two lower). The whiskers begin in empty blur with nothing to attach to, so they read as loose hairs floating beside the cloud rather than flagella growing out of a cell. The dashes are uniformly sized, randomly rotated and sit on TOP of the blur at full opacity — classic sprayed-on speckle, not internal structure. Asymmetric filament placement (right side only) makes it look like a rendering accident.
rows.fix: Give the colony an actual boundary: draw one irregular, lobed membrane path (perlin-warped, not a blur field) and clip the blur and speckle INSIDE it so the edge is the cell's edge, not the falloff of a shadow. Root the filaments on that path — start each curve ON the boundary with a thickened base that tapers, and distribute them around the full perimeter (or make one-sided tufting a deliberate polar tuft with many more, shorter hairs). Modulate the rod dashes by depth: reduce alpha and add blur to rods that sit under the thicker part of the cloud so they read as suspended in cytoplasm rather than printed on the front.

rows.readsAs: A bicycle wheel, or a radar sweep screen. Not remotely biological.
rows.defect: This is not an organism, it is a polar coordinate grid. A geometrically perfect outer circle, 16 dead-straight radial spokes at exact equal angles, and 3 perfect concentric rings, over a flat blue-grey radial gradient with a small grey disc at the hub. Every prohibited primitive is present at once: perfect circle, straight machined edges, exact rotational symmetry, uniform 1px stroke weight with no thick/thin variation. There is no cytoplasm, no membrane thickness, no asymmetry, no nucleus, no organelles, nothing that varies. It is also a hue-swap twin of microbe-h2-s19 in this same batch — identical geometry, purple instead of white.
rows.fix: Kill the perfect-circle path: warp the outer boundary with 2-3 octaves of low-frequency noise so the radius varies 6-10% and no two lobes match. Jitter spoke angles by ±4-6 degrees and vary spoke count so it is not a factor of 16; give each spoke a tapering width (thick at the rim, vanishing near the hub) and let them curve slightly rather than run dead straight. Break the concentric rings into discontinuous arcs of differing thickness. Then add what makes it alive: an off-centre nucleus, a few unevenly sized vacuoles, granular cytoplasm texture. If the intent is a radiolarian/diatom, use real diatom valve structure — a hexagonal areolae field with a raphe slit, not a wagon wheel.

rows.readsAs: A string of pink bubblegum beads or bubble-shooter balls. A generous viewer might say streptococcus, but only from the chain arrangement.
rows.defect: Eleven identical spheres in two chains on a bare background. Each sphere is a mathematically perfect circle with an identical flat pink-to-magenta gradient and an identical white specular hotspot in the same relative upper-left position on every single ball — the giveaway of a reused primitive. Where spheres touch, they simply overlap with a hard edge; there is no shared cell wall, no flattening at the contact face, no septum, so they read as loose beads rather than a dividing chain. The two chains are unconnected and the short 3-ball chain floats in the upper-left corner with no relationship to the main one, leaving the composition visually broken. No surface texture, no capsule, no internal contents.
rows.fix: Make them cells, not balls. Deform each coccus with per-cell noise so no two outlines match and none is a true circle; flatten the faces where neighbours meet and draw a visible septum line at each junction so the chain reads as one dividing organism. Replace the identical specular hotspot with a soft wet sheen whose position and size varies per cell, and drop specular strength substantially — the current hotspot is plastic. Add faint granular cytoplasm and a slightly darker cell-wall rim. Connect or remove the orphan 3-ball chain, and centre the mass; as composed, the lower-right chain runs off toward the frame edge.

rows.readsAs: Sperm cells, or flagellate protozoa such as Trypanosoma. The read is correct and immediate.
rows.defect: The best image in the batch. Three orange-red teardrop cells with long sinuous flagella; the tails genuinely emerge from the narrow pole and taper, with no seam — this one passes the growth test. Remaining faults are modest: the body outlines are near-perfect symmetric teardrops, all three built from the same shape at different scales and rotations, so they read as three copies rather than three individuals. The internal nucleus is a single flat soft-edged blob in each with no other organelles. The bottom-centre flagellum crosses and loops in a way that makes its ownership ambiguous — at a glance it looks like a stray hair between the lower-left and lower-centre cells. Surface is a smooth gradient with no membrane texture.
rows.fix: Add per-cell asymmetry — bulge one flank, vary the taper rate — so the three silhouettes are not the same curve. Route the lower-centre flagellum so it does not cross the lower-left cell's tail, or add depth (slight blur plus alpha reduction on the one passing behind) to disambiguate. Add a second internal feature (a kinetoplast or a couple of small vacuoles) and a faint undulating-membrane ridge along one side so the body is not a pure gradient.

rows.readsAs: A cloud of amber dust or spice, lit from within. Not identifiable as an organism.
rows.defect: A straight palette swap of microbe-h2-s12 — same blur-field body, same speckle distribution, same four whisker filaments leaving the right edge only — recoloured amber/gold with warmer, denser rod dashes and a scatter of grey translucent discs. Same structural failure: no membrane, no silhouette, no boundary anywhere, just overlapping soft gaussians whose outer falloff IS the edge. The grey discs are perfect flat circles at uniform opacity sitting on top of the blur like lens dust. The filaments again start in empty haze with no attachment point. Having two near-identical images in one batch also collapses the perceived variety of the procedural router.
rows.fix: Same fix as s12 — clip to an irregular noise-warped membrane and root the filaments on that path with tapering bases — plus differentiate this seed from s12 structurally, not only by hue: change lobe count, filament count and placement, and speckle density, or the two seeds will keep rendering as the same picture. Replace the perfect grey discs with irregular, unevenly sized vacuoles that pick up the surrounding amber and sit inside the cytoplasm rather than over it.

rows.readsAs: A tardigrade / water bear. Correctly identifiable, but it reads as a toy or a vector icon of one rather than a specimen.
rows.defect: The read is right — a tardigrade — but the construction is assembly, not growth. The body is a plain ellipse; the head is a smaller separate rounded lobe pasted onto the right end, and its outline arc is visible crossing the body where the two shapes overlap, so the head looks stuck on rather than continuous with the trunk. The four legs are simple tapered pegs meeting the underside of the ellipse at an abrupt hard join with no muscle mass, no haunch, no shared contour. The segmentation is five dead-straight vertical strokes drawn across the body; they ignore the ellipse's curvature entirely and read as pinstripes painted on top instead of the ridges between real segments. The two dark facial circles are perfect flat discs. A hard bright rim highlight along the upper-left edge reads as a stroke rather than light.
rows.fix: Build trunk and head as one continuous path with a slight cephalic constriction instead of two overlapping shapes — no outline may cross the body. Grow the legs from the trunk: widen each base and blend it into the belly contour so the silhouette bulges outward rather than sprouting. Curve the segment lines to follow the body's cross-section (bow them and let them wrap toward the silhouette at each end), vary their spacing, and drop them to a soft shaded crease rather than a hard stroke. Deform the ellipse itself with noise so the back is uneven and the belly sags. Soften the rim highlight into a gradient and give the claws real hooked tips.

rows.readsAs: A paramecium. The identification lands, but it looks like a textbook diagram rather than a living cell.
rows.defect: Recognisable as a ciliate, but every shape in it is a drafting primitive. The body is a mathematically perfect ellipse rotated about 35 degrees — a pure geometric form with no asymmetry, no oral groove, no anterior/posterior difference, so the creature has no front. The cilia are near-identical straight hairs of uniform length and even angular spacing rimming the entire outline like a scrub-brush border; real ciliature varies in length and bends into metachronal waves. Inside, three thin-stroke PERFECT circles sit as vacuoles, drawn at compass precision with uniform 1px outlines and no fill difference from the cytoplasm, and there is a stray dead-straight horizontal line segment to the left of them that connects to nothing and reads as a rendering artifact. The dark central oval is the only organic-looking element.
rows.fix: Replace the ellipse with an asymmetric slipper outline — blunt anterior, tapered posterior, with a concave oral groove indenting one flank — and warp the boundary with low-frequency noise. Vary cilia length, curvature and density around the perimeter, curving them into a directional wave and lengthening them at the posterior; a few should visibly pass in front of the body. Make the vacuoles irregular blobs of varying size with a faint refractive fill and rim shading, not compass circles. Delete the stray horizontal line. Add granular cytoplasm and a food vacuole trail so the interior is not a flat gradient.

rows.readsAs: A purple wagon wheel or a dartboard. There is nothing biological in it.
rows.defect: Not an organism — the identical polar-grid construction as microbe-h2-s13, recoloured purple. Perfect outer circle, 16 exactly equal straight radial spokes, 3 perfect concentric rings, flat radial gradient fill, small disc at the hub. Perfect rotational symmetry, uniform stroke weight, zero asymmetry, zero organic variation, no nucleus or organelles. Shipping two hue-swapped copies of a wagon wheel as two distinct species is the worst outcome in this batch.
rows.fix: Same structural rebuild as s13 — noise-warp the outer boundary, jitter and taper the spokes, break the rings into arcs of varying weight, add an off-centre nucleus and irregular vacuoles — and additionally make this seed diverge from s13 in geometry, not just hue (different rib count, different boundary noise, different internal contents), otherwise the router keeps emitting the same picture twice. If a radial body plan is genuinely intended, model an actual radiolarian: an irregular siliceous lattice with spines of varying length radiating past the boundary.

rows.readsAs: Cyan medicine capsules, or a Tetris L-piece next to a dash and two bars
rows.defect: These are not cells, they are pharmaceutical gel capsules. Seven identical-width cyan capsules float loose on the canvas; at 4x zoom each one carries a hard straight seam line drawn across its middle exactly where a two-piece medicine capsule joins, plus a glossy vertical specular stripe running the whole length like moulded plastic. The three 'bent' rods are not bent at all — a second capsule is laid ON TOP of the first at an angle, leaving a hard crescent seam at the elbow (visible at 140,270). Every silhouette is a perfect stadium/capsule shape with a mathematically constant radius; nothing tapers, nothing varies, no cell wall, no pole, no division furrow. The seven bodies also have no compositional relationship — three float in a row across the top like a dash-and-bars glyph, four pile in the lower right — so the frame reads as scattered props rather than a colony.
rows.fix: Kill the capsule primitive outright. Build each bacillus from a spline centre-line with a width profile that swells mid-body and rounds asymmetrically at the poles, and jitter length/width/curvature per cell so no two match. Delete the mid-body seam line and the full-length gloss stripe — replace with a soft broad rim-light down one side only. Bent rods must be ONE continuous curved centre-line, never two overlaid capsules. Add a real dividing constriction (a pinch in the width profile) on one or two cells so the shape says 'fission' instead of 'pill'. Reduce to 4-5 cells and cluster them with a shared drift direction.

rows.readsAs: A pink smoke plume, or a stained microscope slide someone photographed out of focus
rows.defect: There is no organism in this picture — it is a magenta fog that fills and bleeds off all four edges of the 440px frame, with roughly a hundred tiny pink dashes and a dozen flat opaque grey discs scattered through it. The grey discs are perfect circles with zero shading, sitting flat on top of the haze like UI dots. The only structure with any drawing in it is a set of long tapering tendrils on the RIGHT SIDE ONLY, and at 3x zoom (300,130) those tendrils are sliced clean off by the canvas edge — the subject is cropped. The tendrils also branch from junction points floating in the fog with nothing at the junction: they attach to haze, not to a body. Nothing here has a silhouette, a centre, or a readable scale.
rows.fix: Give it a body. Composite the haze as a bounded colony mass with a soft but findable outline, inset ~12% from every edge so nothing clips. Anchor every flagellum/tendril to an actual cell on the mass and taper it to zero width before it reaches the frame — no cropped appendages. Distribute the tendrils around the whole perimeter, not just the right. Replace the flat grey discs with shaded interior vesicles that pick up the magenta ambient, or drop them. Vary the rod flecks in length and opacity by depth so the field has near/far instead of one uniform confetti layer.

rows.readsAs: A string of blue pop-beads or bath pearls
rows.defect: A string of plastic pop-beads. Two disjoint chains of identical mid-blue spheres, roughly 6 and 8 balls, with no relationship to each other and no third element to tie the composition. At 4x (235,90) every sphere is the same radius and carries the SAME top-left specular hotspot at the SAME position, so the light reads as pasted per-ball rather than falling across the chain. Where balls meet there is a hard crescent seam — one sphere simply overlaps the next, with no shared cell wall, no flattening at the contact, no septum. The chains are also empty inside: pure radial gradient, no cytoplasmic texture, no membrane edge.
rows.fix: Flatten each coccus where it contacts its neighbour (contact patches, not overlaps) and draw a single septum line across the flat, so the chain reads as cells that divided rather than beads threaded on wire. Vary radius +/-15% down the chain and let the newest cells be smaller. Light the whole chain from one direction — the specular must migrate around the balls as the chain curves. Add faint interior granularity and a slightly darker membrane rim. Merge the two chains into one branching streptococcus, or make the second chain clearly younger/smaller so the frame has a subject.

rows.readsAs: A pink party streamer, or a sawtooth waveform on an oscilloscope
rows.defect: The spirochete is a sawtooth, not a helix. At 4x (100,120) the pink ribbon turns through sharp angular corners — hard Vs and near-right-angle kinks — at a dead-constant width, which is a waveform, not a coiling body. Edges are visibly aliased in places (stair-stepped pixels along the diagonals) while others are soft, so the stroke reads as a marker line rather than a rendered form. The colour is applied as flat alternating blocks of light pink and darker magenta along the stroke, chunks that ignore the curve entirely — sprayed-on banding, not skin. The thin dark flagella are near-black on a near-black field and read as scratches on the canvas rather than as filaments; several start in empty space with no visible attachment to the ribbon. Two separate coils overlap in the middle with no depth cue about which is in front.
rows.fix: Generate the coil as a smooth sinusoid/helix with a curvature limit — no corner may exceed ~60 degrees — and taper the ribbon width to a point at both ends. Make the width breathe slightly along the length so it reads as a body under tension. Replace the flat colour blocks with lighting that follows the coil: crest highlights and trough shadows derived from the tangent normal, so the banding IS the 3D form. Re-colour the flagella to a lighter tint of the body (they must be visible against the dark plate) and attach each one to a pole of the ribbon with a tapered root. Add a depth darken where one coil passes behind another.

rows.readsAs: A planet icon or a snow globe — a UI glyph, not a living thing
rows.defect: This is a snow globe, not a microbe. At 4x (150,155) it is a mathematically perfect circle outlined with a uniform 1px light-grey stroke — a machined edge — filled with a smooth grey-green radial gradient. The bottom third is cut off by a RAZOR-STRAIGHT horizontal chord below which sits a flat, completely unshaded green fill with no gradient and no texture, exactly like liquid in a glass bead. A perfect white circle sits at the upper left like a moon, and five flat green dots float in the upper field. Nothing about this has a membrane, an appendage, a nucleus, or an axis. It is also badly under-scaled — the disc occupies roughly a quarter of the 440px frame while every other organism in the batch fills half or more.
rows.fix: Delete the outline stroke and the straight chord entirely. Rebuild as a real cell: an irregular, slightly non-circular membrane (perlin-perturbed radius) with a soft thickened rim rather than a hairline; a shaded, off-centre organelle mass instead of the flat green cap; and interior granules that sit IN the gradient with their own tiny shadows rather than as flat dots. Replace the white 'moon' disc with a broad soft specular that follows the membrane curvature. Scale the subject up to ~55-65% of frame height to match the batch.

rows.readsAs: A tardigrade — recognisable, though a casual viewer might say cartoon hippo or manatee
rows.defect: Closest thing to a real animal in the batch — it does read as a tardigrade — but it is a plain egg with parts stuck on. At 4x (240,150) the head is a separate rounded lump laid over the right end of the body, and the head's own dark outline continues DOWN ACROSS the body as a hard seam line: a visible join, not a neck. The two eyespots are flat black ellipses of different sizes floating on the surface with no socket, lid or rim. At 4x (100,130) the back carries a bright desaturated grey-white rim stroke that reads as glossy plastic or glass, not cuticle. The 'segmentation' is four or five dead-straight, perfectly vertical, uniform-width hairlines that ignore the barrel's curvature completely and stop abruptly mid-body — sprayed on top of the form rather than being creases in it. Under the animal is a hard flat black ellipse doing duty as a shadow. The legs are the one good part: they genuinely taper out of the body and end in claw tufts.
rows.fix: Merge the head into the body with a metaball/union so the outline is one continuous contour with a soft shoulder — no crossing seam. Set the eyespots into the head: match the pair's size, add a darker socket ring and a tiny specular. Re-draw the segmentation as curved bands that follow the barrel's cross-section (arcs that bow with the silhouette and fade at both ends into the shading), not vertical straight lines. Desaturate-and-tint the rim light to the body hue instead of grey-white, and reduce its intensity. Replace the black ellipse with a soft contact shadow that is darkest under the feet and dissipates outward.

rows.readsAs: A string of green beads in a Y — indistinguishable from microbe-h1-s18 apart from colour
rows.defect: Same generator as microbe-h1-s18, recoloured green — a viewer shown both would say they are the same organism twice. Chains of identical perfect spheres, each with the identical top-left highlight, overlapped rather than joined so a hard crescent seam sits at every contact. Here they meet in a Y: one chain runs to the upper right, one to the left, one drops straight down, and the junction is just three balls piled on the same spot with no branch structure — the down-chain has no visible parent cell, it simply starts under the pile. Ball radius is constant across all three arms so there is no sense of growth direction or age. The spheres are hollow-looking, pure gradient with no interior.
rows.fix: Differentiate this from s18 morphologically, not by hue: make it a genuine branching filament with a thicker, larger parent cell at the junction that the three arms visibly bud from, and taper the cells smaller toward each tip. Flatten the contact patches and add septa. Rotate the specular around each cell to follow one global light. Add interior granularity and a membrane rim. If the two species really are meant to share a body plan, one of them must change chain count, cell shape (ovoid vs round) or clustering pattern.

rows.readsAs: Peanuts or a cluster of potatoes sitting in front of a firework burst
rows.defect: The body is smothered by a sunburst that does not belong to it. At 4x (170,160) roughly a hundred dead-straight, uniform-width hairlines radiate from a single vanishing point that sits OUTSIDE the cell cluster, so most of them are floating in empty black space with no attachment to anything — a textbook off-body artifact, and where they do cross the cells they pass in front like scratches on the lens. The cluster itself is six or seven perfect tan spheres overlapped with hard crescent seams at every contact, no flattening, no shared wall. The largest sphere has a flat dark ellipse punched into it, no rim and no depth, like a hole cut in paper. The surface speckling is a uniform random dot spray applied at the same density and size regardless of the sphere's curvature, so it does not wrap the form. Colour is a flat sandy tan with almost no hue variation — it reads as peanuts.
rows.fix: Anchor the radiating structures: emit each spine from a point ON a cell surface, give it a tapered root that fattens where it meets the membrane, curve it slightly, and vary length and thickness. Cut the count by two-thirds. Nothing may originate in empty space or from a shared vanishing point. Flatten sphere contacts into real junctions with septa. Replace the punched ellipse with a shaded pore — darkened rim, gradient interior, a lip catching the key light. Make the speckle density fall off toward the silhouette edges so it follows the curvature, and push some hue variation (warm crown, cooler shadow side) into the tan.
